title: Preface
summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s 2022 Form 10-K identifies the registrant, fiscal year, corporate and contact details, listed common and preferred securities, exchange listings, and filing status. It reports market value, shares outstanding, and proxy-statement material incorporated by reference. The index outlines Parts I–IV, covering the business and segments, regulation, financial and risk information, legal matters, market and operating results, financial statements, controls, governance, executive compensation, ownership, related transactions, audit fees, and exhibits.

title: Item 1. Business.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase Business, Segments, and Competition
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase is a U.S.-based global financial holding company with $3.7 trillion in assets at year-end 2022, serving consumers, businesses, and institutions through banking and other financial services. The page outlines its principal U.S. and international subsidiaries, website access to SEC filings and company information, and employee and executive ethics codes. Its reporting segments are Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, Asset & Wealth Management, and Corporate. It also describes broad competition across financial and technology industries, with firms competing on service, execution, innovation, reputation, and price across global, national, and regional markets.

Firm culture; Attracting and retaining employees; Developing employees
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its human-capital strategy, covering its 293,723 employees across 63 countries, workforce growth and regional/business distribution, and self-reported diversity statistics with definitions and scope. It outlines its values, inclusive culture, employee resource groups and DEI centers; recruitment, internal mobility, hybrid work, diverse hiring and return-to-work fellowships; onboarding, training and leadership development; and performance-oriented, equitable compensation and extensive health, wellness, leave, retirement and other benefits. It also notes the Firm is subject to comprehensive U.S. and international regulation.

Holding company as a source of strength
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase is a federally supervised bank and financial holding company, with U.S. and international subsidiaries regulated by relevant banking, securities, and derivatives authorities. The text outlines limits and eligibility conditions on financial activities; capital, liquidity, leverage, stress-testing, and enhanced prudential requirements; recovery and resolution planning and orderly liquidation; the parent’s duty to support bank subsidiaries; acquisition restrictions and approvals; and ongoing obligations under a 2020 DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement and related CFTC order.

FDIC powers upon a bank insolvency

nodes.summary: The text outlines regulatory requirements affecting JPMorgan Chase’s subsidiary banks, including OCC enforcement and heightened risk-governance standards; FDIC insurance, insolvency powers, prompt corrective action and capital-restoration guarantees; affiliate-transaction and dividend limits; and depositor priority. It covers U.S. and U.K. consumer-protection supervision, including a proposed CFPB cap on credit-card late fees, as well as regulation of securities and broker-dealer activities, investment management and fiduciary services, and derivatives—including capital, margin, clearing, trading, reporting and swap-dealer rules.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase Regulatory Oversight and Restrictions
nodes.summary: The page describes bank risk-governance oversight and federal restrictions on affiliate transactions, dividends, and creditor priority, plus U.S. and U.K. consumer-protection supervision, including a proposed CFPB cap on credit-card late fees. It outlines regulation of the Firm’s securities underwriting, dealing, and brokerage activities, and global asset- and wealth-management rules covering client assets, funds, marketing, investment-adviser duties, and bank fiduciary activities.

nodes.title: Derivatives regulation:
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan’s regulatory obligations across derivatives, data and cybersecurity, anti-money-laundering and sanctions, anti-corruption, compensation, and international financial-market reforms. It describes dealer and futures commission merchant registrations; associated capital, margin, clearing, trading, collateral, conduct, reporting, and recordkeeping rules; evolving global data protections; BSA and OFAC, EU, U.K., and other sanctions requirements; anti-bribery laws; oversight of incentive compensation; and MiFID II reforms in the EU and U.K., including proposed transparency, market-structure, and trading changes.

It covers evolving global data, privacy and cybersecurity rules; BSA anti-money-laundering, counter-terrorism financing, record-keeping and customer due diligence duties; OFAC, EU, U.K. and other sanctions, including conflicting requirements; anti-corruption laws such as the FCPA and U.K. Bribery Act; and U.S., international and CRD V oversight of compensation practices to curb imprudent risk-taking, with rules and their effects continuing to evolve.

nodes.title: Other significant international regulatory initiatives:
nodes.summary: The text outlines ongoing U.K. and EU financial regulatory reforms: MiFID II changes to trading, transparency, market structure and reporting, including an EU consolidated tape and U.K. Wholesale Markets Review; proposed EMIR clearing reforms and delayed CSDR buy-in rules; the U.K. Edinburgh Reforms; and Basel III rules due by 2025, with transition periods, revised risk calculations, stronger EU supervision and ESG requirements. It also covers EU IPU obligations, supervisory expectations for climate, technology, operational resilience and external shocks, and sustainability measures: expanded CSRD reporting from 2024 and proposed CSDDD human-rights, environmental and climate-plan due diligence, applicable to certain Firm entities.

summary: Describes JPMorgan Chase’s global business, subsidiaries, reporting segments, workforce and human-capital policies, and competition. Covers its status as a regulated financial holding company and the extensive U.S., U.K. and international rules governing its parent and subsidiary banks, including capital, liquidity, governance, resolution, acquisitions, consumer protection, securities, asset management and fiduciary services. Also addresses derivatives, privacy and cybersecurity, AML and sanctions, anti-corruption, compensation, MiFID II, EMIR, Basel III, U.K./EU reforms, climate and sustainability requirements, and related compliance obligations.

title: Item 1A. Risk Factors.

nodes.title: Summary
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase warns that the listed material risks are not exhaustive and that any risk, alone or combined, could materially harm its business, results, financial condition, capital, liquidity, competitiveness or reputation, increasing expenses, reducing revenue or causing losses. Principal risks include regulatory and political developments; market and credit conditions; liquidity, funding, ratings and reference-rate transitions; capital requirements; operational systems, staffing, cybersecurity, privacy, models, controls and vendors; strategy, competition and climate change; employee conduct and reputation; country conditions and conflict; attracting and retaining employees and immigration policies; and litigation and government or regulatory investigations.

nodes.title: Regulatory JPMorgan Chase’s businesses are highly regulated, and the laws, rules and regulations that apply to JPMorgan Chase have a significant impact on its business and operations.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase operates worldwide under extensive financial regulation and supervision, which shapes its business and operations and may require changes as laws, rules, expectations, or business activities evolve. Compliance can raise costs and reduce profitability. Requirements may limit products, services, market-making liquidity, or business opportunities; increase taxes, levies, or losses; force disadvantageous asset sales or activity restrictions; and raise prices, reducing demand. Noncompliance may trigger heightened scrutiny, enforcement, fines or sanctions, litigation exposure, and reputational harm.

nodes.title: Differences and inconsistencies in financial services regulation can negatively impact JPMorgan Chase’s businesses, operations and financial results.
nodes.summary: Differences in financial regulation by firm size, jurisdiction, and business type can subject JPMorgan Chase to stricter oversight than competitors, create competitive disadvantages, and cause conflicts between U.S. and foreign laws. International requirements may force operational or legal-entity changes involving local subsidiaries, capital and liquidity, ring-fencing, resolution, trading and derivatives, governance, conduct, and compensation. Resulting impacts may include divestitures or restructuring, higher capital, compliance and operating costs, changed prices or reduced services and opportunities, and sanctions—potentially weakening competitiveness, operations, results, and profitability.

nodes.title: Resolving regulatory investigations can subject JPMorgan Chase to significant penalties and collateral consequences, and could result in higher compliance costs or restrictions on its operations.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces heightened regulatory scrutiny, fines, remediation costs, operating restrictions, and reputational, litigation, client, and business consequences from investigations and enforcement actions, including potential criminal admissions or guilty pleas. It expects continued formal enforcement and greater scrutiny after prior actions; failure to meet resolutions or regulatory standards could bring further penalties, restrictions, prosecution, or litigation. Less predictable legal systems abroad create compliance challenges, unexpected outcomes, and potential earnings and operational harm. Federal Reserve and FDIC resolution-plan requirements may force structural changes, raise costs, restrict activities, or require divestitures. The text also notes that Parent Company debt and equity holders would absorb losses in a resolution.

nodes.title: Regulatory, Legal, and Resolution Risks
key_items: JPMorgan Chase’s operations and financial results can be negatively impacted in countries with less predictable legal and regulatory frameworks.

Requirements for the orderly resolution of JPMorgan Chase could result in JPMorgan Chase having to restructure or reorganize its businesses and could increase its funding or operational costs or curtail its businesses.
nodes.summary: The text describes heightened government scrutiny and enforcement risks, including repeat investigations, penalties, restrictions, litigation, or prosecution if JPMorgan Chase violates resolutions or fails to meet regulatory standards. Unpredictable legal and regulatory frameworks abroad may complicate compliance, require added resources, and harm operations and earnings. Resolution-plan requirements may prompt structural or business changes, raise costs, limit client service or growth, or require divestitures and stricter capital, leverage, or liquidity rules.

nodes.title: Holders of JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s debt and equity securities will absorb losses if it were to enter into a resolution.
nodes.summary: Federal Reserve rules require JPMorgan Chase’s parent company to maintain eligible unsecured long-term debt and other loss-absorbing capacity to recapitalize subsidiaries if it enters Chapter 11 bankruptcy or FDIC Title II receivership. Under the preferred single-point-of-entry plan, only the parent enters bankruptcy and subsidiaries are recapitalized, sold, or wound down; parent equity absorbs losses first, followed by unsecured creditors. Their claims rank behind subsidiary creditors and the parent’s priority and secured creditors, and recoveries depend on value received from subsidiaries after priority and secured claims are paid. The FDIC has described this approach as potentially desirable under Title II but has not formally adopted it. No party is required to follow JPMorgan’s preferred strategy, and losses to parent-company security holders could be greater under another approach.

nodes.title: Political Economic uncertainty or instability caused by political developments can negatively impact JPMorgan Chase’s businesses.
nodes.summary: Political developments, policy shifts, geopolitical tensions and uncertainty may disrupt economic growth and markets, undermining confidence, government support or funding, and affecting counterparties or JPMorgan Chase’s business choices. Outcomes may include recession or inflation, volatility, tighter credit, asset sales, trade contraction, currency or alliance changes, expropriation and wider market dislocations, causing losses, reduced liquidity or capital, higher credit losses, service disruption and weaker results. Conflicting government directives on financial institutions’ dealings with sensitive industries or required practices may trigger restrictions, enforcement, reputational damage, and harm to client or government relationships; ESG or industry affiliations may also be viewed as discriminatory or politically aligned.

nodes.title: Market Economic and market events and conditions can materially affect JPMorgan Chase’s businesses and investment and market-making positions.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s results may be harmed by shifts in sentiment, financial-market confidence, economic conditions, employment, capital, liquidity and credit availability or cost, interest rates, spreads, and currency, equity, and commodity prices and volatility. Geopolitical events, cyberattacks, climate and natural disasters, severe weather, health emergencies, pandemics, other extraordinary events, global economic and political conditions, and regulation can also affect results. Investment and market-making losses may result from sharp asset declines, unexpected credit events, changing correlations, ineffective hedging, or unaccounted-for risks in financial instruments. Significant losses could reduce profitability, liquidity, and capital, limiting business growth.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s consumer businesses can be negatively affected by adverse economic conditions and governmental policies.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s consumer businesses are vulnerable to U.S. and global economic conditions, including income distribution, unemployment, interest rates, housing prices, inflation, consumer and small-business confidence, spending, and debt. Weak conditions can reduce customers’ ability to repay, dampen demand, increase delinquencies, credit-loss allowances and charge-offs, and lower earnings, especially in hard-hit industries or areas and where high debt, including student loans, strains repayment. Government policies affecting health insurance, education, immigration, employment and housing, as well as broader measures such as higher taxes and regulation that reduce disposable income, may also hurt earnings.

nodes.title: Unfavorable market and economic conditions can have an adverse effect on JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale businesses.
nodes.summary: Adverse market and economic conditions can reduce JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale transaction volumes, fees, capital-markets profitability, and ability to sell credit commitments, while increasing residual exposures and credit losses. Sector-specific shocks can harm clients and their ability to repay. Falling asset values, fund outflows, or shifts to lower-revenue products can reduce asset-management and custody fees and trigger further withdrawals. Economic downturns and changing spending patterns may also weaken wholesale clients—especially commercial real estate borrowers—causing lower rental income and property values, impaired repayment or refinancing, and higher credit-loss allowances, delinquencies, defaults, charge-offs, and loan-servicing costs.

nodes.title: Changes in interest rates and credit spreads can adversely affect JPMorgan Chase’s earnings, its liquidity or its capital levels.
nodes.summary: Interest-rate and credit-spread changes can affect JPMorgan Chase’s earnings, liquidity, and capital. Higher rates may boost net interest income but can reduce real-estate lending, cause client credit losses and delinquencies, trigger deposit outflows, produce losses on available-for-sale securities, lower income through rate-pricing mismatches, reduce market liquidity, and raise funding costs. Low or negative rates may compress margins, alter depositor behavior, and reduce mortgage-servicing-rights values. Wider credit spreads increase borrowing costs; spread movements driven by company-specific or broader economic and geopolitical conditions also affect the fair value and earnings of certain liabilities, including derivatives.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s results may be materially affected by market fluctuations and significant changes in the value of financial instruments.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s results may be harmed by market fluctuations, volatility, illiquidity, and financial-market disruptions that make securities, derivatives, and other instruments difficult to value. Future valuations or sale prices may be materially lower than current fair value, reducing the value of holdings or instruments it makes markets in. Risk monitoring and stress testing seek to quantify and manage exposure to extreme moves, but hedging and other controls may fail, resulting in significant losses.

nodes.title: Credit JPMorgan Chase can be negatively affected by adverse changes in the financial condition of clients, counterparties, custodians and CCPs.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces credit, operational, legal and reputational risks from client, counterparty, custodian and CCP defaults or failures, including collateral shortfalls, replacement costs, shared CCP losses, disputes, litigation and regulatory investigations. Government actions and local laws may invalidate transactions or hinder recovery. Derivatives disputes over terms, settlement or collateral can cause losses and impair risk management. Failure or perceived weakness of a major market participant can trigger cascading market disruption, liquidity problems and defaults, significantly disrupting JPMorgan Chase given its interconnections and exposures.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase may suffer losses if the value of collateral declines in stressed market conditions.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces increased credit losses when collateral values fall, cannot be realized or liquidated adequately, counterparties fail to post collateral, or valuation disputes arise during market stress. Concentrated exposures to related clients, industries, regions or business models can trigger contagion, fair-value losses and higher credit-loss allowances; monitoring may not overcome limited diversification or hedging. Consumer-credit competition and excessive lending may lead to defaults, charge-offs, recession and lower revenue. Difficulty reducing positions can raise market and credit risk, risk-weighted assets, funding costs and pressure on capital and profitability. Liquidity may be impaired by market disruption, unexpected needs or outflows, asset-sale difficulties, participant defaults, or loss of confidence. Reduced access to stable funding may force costlier alternatives, while regulatory liquidity, resolution and subsidiary pre-positioning requirements can raise costs. Poor liquidity management may constrain business funding and investment and harm results.

nodes.title: Credit, Market Risk Concentrations and Liquidity
key_items: JPMorgan Chase could incur significant losses arising from concentrations of credit and market risk.
Liquidity JPMorgan Chase’s ability to operate its businesses could be impaired if its liquidity is constrained.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase may incur losses when related clients, industries or regions face shared economic pressures, through contagion, collateral declines, credit-loss allowances, consumer defaults, competitive lending practices, or difficulty reducing positions; diversification and hedging may be limited, affecting risk-weighted assets, capital, funding costs and profits. Liquidity may be constrained by market disruption, unexpected requirements or outflows, asset-sale limits, defaults, or loss of confidence. Reduced access to stable funding may force costlier alternatives, including to meet regulatory and resolution-plan requirements, potentially limiting business operations and harming results.

nodes.title: Holding Company Dependence and Credit Rating Risks
key_items: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a holding company and depends on the cash flows of its subsidiaries to make payments on its outstanding securities.
Reductions in JPMorgan Chase’s credit ratings may adversely affect its liquidity and cost of funding.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co. relies on subsidiaries for cash to meet its obligations, but regulatory, capital, and liquidity limits on subsidiary dividends and lending may hinder debt interest, equity dividends, security repurchases, and other payments, potentially prompting earlier bankruptcy or resolution. Credit ratings reflect financial, operational, regulatory, and broader economic factors; downgrades, which cannot be ruled out, could restrict business and market access, raise funding and collateral costs, reduce counterparties and investors, and lower the value of company and subsidiary obligations.

nodes.title: The transition to alternative reference rates could expose JPMorgan Chase to operational risks or litigation and other disputes.
nodes.summary: The shift from LIBOR and other benchmarks to alternative rates such as SOFR may not preserve equivalent economics or achieve broad acceptance, and ineffective transitions could disrupt markets, increase volatility, suppress capital-market activity, and harm JPMorgan Chase and related instruments. The transition may also trigger client, counterparty, and investor disputes alleging unfair treatment, inadequate disclosure, unsuitable recommendations, anticompetitive conduct or market manipulation, or unfavorable contract interpretations, increasing costs and reputational harm. Separately, regulatory leverage- and risk-based capital requirements and GSIB buffers may rise because of regulatory actions, systemic events, balance-sheet or risk changes, or stress-test losses. Failure to meet capital requirements could limit buybacks and dividends, require or restrict capital issuance or redemption, and constrain business activity.

nodes.title: Operational JPMorgan Chase’s businesses are dependent on the effectiveness of its operational systems and those of other market participants.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase depends on reliable, secure, accurate and well-maintained operational systems—including systems of vendors, custodians and market infrastructures—to process transactions and meet legal and regulatory requirements. Failures, cyberattacks, corrupted data or disruptions could delay services and settlements, cause erroneous transactions and financial losses, raise costs, limit regulatory data collection, trigger sanctions, undermine customer confidence and damage its reputation. Growing transaction speed, volume and complexity heighten risks from fraud, errors, cascading failures, software or hardware problems, and intellectual-property claims. Inadequate systems at JPMorgan Chase, acquired businesses or external parties could materially harm the firm.

nodes.title: A successful cyber attack affecting JPMorgan Chase could cause significant harm to JPMorgan Chase and its clients and customers.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces frequent, increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks from state-linked actors, criminals, hacktivists, insiders and others, including malware, data theft or manipulation, service disruption, theft, extortion and DDoS attacks; past breaches make future incidents inevitable. Absolute prevention is impossible given evolving threats, external dependencies and undetected network footholds. Risk may rise with digital and cloud expansion, acquisitions, remote work and intercepted mobile communications. Breaches could disrupt operations, expose or destroy data, enable fraud, cause legal, financial, regulatory and reputational harm, and erode customer confidence. Investigations and remediation may be lengthy and uncertain, allowing damage to spread, complicating communications and increasing costs.

nodes.title: Operational, External-System, and Workforce Risks
key_items: JPMorgan Chase can be negatively affected if it fails to identify and address operational risks associated with the introduction of or changes to products, services and delivery platforms.
JPMorgan Chase’s operational costs and customer satisfaction could be adversely affected by the failure of an external operational system.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from failing to identify and control operational risks when launching or changing products, services, platforms, or businesses, potentially causing liability, higher costs, litigation, reputational and liquidity damage, regulatory intervention, and weaker competitiveness. Failures or cyberattacks at connected external parties may enable fraud, create losses and remediation costs, harm reputation and customer confidence, restrict account access, or trigger industry-wide disruption. It also notes reliance on appropriately staffed, competent, trustworthy, healthy, and safe employee and third-party workforces, and begins listing risks including ineffective implementation of business decisions.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s business and operations rely on its ability, and the ability of key external parties, to maintain appropriatelystaffed workforces, and on the competence, trustworthiness, health and safety of employees.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces operational risks when launching or changing products, services, platforms, or businesses without identifying and controlling new risks, potentially causing liability, costs, litigation, reputational or liquidity damage, regulatory intervention, weaker competitiveness, and business harm. Failures or cyberattacks at connected vendors, customers, and financial-market systems can enable fraud, create losses and remediation costs, damage reputation, disrupt operations industry-wide, or require account restrictions that reduce customer confidence. The firm also depends on adequate, competent, trustworthy, healthy, and safe employees and external-party workforces; staffing shortages, health emergencies, poor training or controls, ineffective decisions, misconduct, fraud, or ineffective safety measures can impair its operations and results.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase faces substantial legal and operational risks in the processing and safeguarding of personal information.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces legal, operational, financial and reputational risks from evolving global privacy and data-protection rules and from failures by the firm or external parties to safeguard personal information. Compliance across conflicting jurisdictions can raise costs, require intensive oversight and inefficient systems, and constrain existing or new products and services. Mishandling, unauthorized disclosure or interception may trigger litigation, investigations, fines, sanctions, operational changes, customer or employee losses, and reduced revenue. Publicized incidents are driving stricter rules, including limits on cross-border transfers, affiliate or vendor sharing, data use, and requirements for local storage and processing, increasing costs and complexity and potentially restricting product development, marketing and delivery.

nodes.title: Operational Disruptions and Service Provider Risks
key_items: JPMorgan Chase’s operations, results and reputation could be harmed by occurrences of extraordinary events beyond its control.
Enhanced regulatory and other standards for the oversight of vendors and other service providers can result in higher costs and other potential exposures.
nodes.summary: Extraordinary events beyond JPMorgan Chase’s control—including cyberattacks, outages, disasters, health crises, accidents, and unrest—may disrupt operations and harm its reputation. Its resiliency program may not fully address single, simultaneous, concentrated, or increasingly chronic disruptions. Failures can impede services and transactions, require costly responses, cause losses or injuries, disrupt market infrastructure, and lead to litigation, sanctions, or reputational damage. Enhanced vendor oversight standards also raise costs; inadequate management of providers, outsourcing, or critical functions may harm clients and cause liability, sanctions, lost revenue, higher costs, and reputational harm.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s risk management framework may not be effective in identifying and mitigating every risk to JPMorgan Chase.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s risk framework, governance, data processes, models, estimates and judgments may fail to identify or mitigate risks, causing losses, poor decisions, delayed or inaccurate reporting, costly remediation, legal or regulatory noncompliance and sanctions, customer harm, reputational damage, or reduced confidence. Models rely on historical trends, assumptions and uncertain forecasts that may fail during market stress, illiquidity or unprecedented conditions; technology, data, valuation, formula or review flaws can also impair them. Inaccurate fair-value and expected-credit-loss estimates may increase uncertainty, as during COVID-19, and reduce capital or invite scrutiny. Regulators review certain models used for Basel III risk-weighted assets; rejection may raise capital charges and constrain results or business growth.

nodes.title: Lapses in controls over disclosure or financial reporting could materially affect JPMorgan Chase’s profitability or reputation.
nodes.summary: Weak disclosure or financial-reporting controls could cause inaccurate reporting, harming JPMorgan Chase’s business, finances, market access, reputation, investor confidence, and exposing it to remediation costs, litigation, or regulatory sanctions. Its competitive position, growth, and earnings also depend on management choosing and executing effective strategies amid changing markets, regulations, competition, and stakeholder expectations. Failures in planning, product adaptation, capital allocation, due diligence and integration, stakeholder and ESG concerns, responsiveness, or resource development could impede stability, investment, expense control, and shareholder returns. Disposing of excess facilities may also incur material costs.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase faces significant and increasing competition in the rapidly evolving financial services industry.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces intense, growing U.S. and global competition amid regulatory, technological, public-scrutiny, and economic changes. Competitors include banks, financial firms, finance companies, technology companies, and other nonbanks. E-commerce and new technologies enable nonbanks to offer traditional banking and digital services, while cryptocurrencies and distributed ledgers may disrupt payments, deposits, and other products. Adapting to technology, security, compliance, and customer needs may raise costs and reduce income. Aggressive nonbank lending could take market share and worsen downturns. Competition over products, execution, innovation, reputation, and price may pressure prices, reduce market share and customer retention, and lower revenues; remaining competitive may require more investment and client capital.

nodes.title: The effects of climate change could adversely affect JPMorgan Chase’s business and operations, both directly and as a result of impacts on its clients and customers.
nodes.summary: Climate change may adversely affect JPMorgan Chase directly and through its clients and customers across its global operations, creating physical and transition-related financial risks that can weaken client creditworthiness and increase the bank’s exposure. Physical risks include severe weather and long-term climate shifts, potentially reducing asset values, limiting or raising insurance costs, disrupting operations and supply chains, and causing migration or unemployment. Transition risks from policy, technology, and consumer shifts may strand assets, raise operating, compliance, and energy costs, undermine business models, and damage reputation. Conflicting or inconsistent climate policies and financial regulations across jurisdictions, including extraterritorial enforcement, are additional risks.

nodes.title: Conduct Conduct failure by JPMorgan Chase employees can harm clients and customers, impact market integrity, damage JPMorgan Chase’s reputation and trigger litigation and regulatory action.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase warns that employee misconduct can harm customers, market integrity and its reputation, and lead to litigation or regulatory action. It sets conduct expectations through its Code, principles, and employee lifecycle, promotion and compensation processes, but past misconduct has led to investigations, settlements and sanctions; future misconduct may occur or evade detection and breach existing resolutions. Examples include mis-selling, trading abuses, relief-program fraud, questionable transaction structuring, fiduciary failures, antitrust violations, unapproved communications, discrimination or harassment, subordinating risk controls to business goals, and misappropriation. Consequences may include losses, costs, scrutiny, restrictions or restructuring, management oversight, customer attrition and reputational damage. Risks may increase when integrating acquired businesses.

nodes.title: Reputation Damage to JPMorgan Chase’s reputation could harm its businesses.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s reputation is essential to retaining clients, investors and employees, and can be harmed by misconduct, discrimination or harassment, security and privacy failures, poor risk management, unmet ESG commitments, legal or regulatory noncompliance, operational failures, sanctions, crisis-response actions, investigations, or perceived failures by the bank and its affiliates, clients, counterparties and vendors. False or true negative publicity can spread rapidly online and through media. Activist criticism and protests over ESG practices and relationships with sensitive industries may prompt stakeholder dissatisfaction. Reputational damage can bring regulatory scrutiny, lost or reduced client relationships, hiring and retention difficulties, investor divestment, or other business and financial harm. Industry-wide concerns about unfair treatment or inappropriate product sales can also damage the bank’s reputation if it is perceived to share those practices.

nodes.title: Failure to effectively manage potential conflicts of interest or to satisfy fiduciary obligations can result in litigation and enforcement actions, as well as damage JPMorgan Chase’s reputation.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s complex business activities create potential conflicts of interest and fiduciary risks. Failures or perceived failures to disclose and manage conflicts, address third-party conflicts, meet service and fairness standards, responsibly use client data, comply with fiduciary requirements, or protect confidential information could trigger customer dissatisfaction, litigation, regulatory scrutiny, fines or sanctions, lost revenue, higher costs, and reputational harm. Country or regional hostilities, including armed conflict and cyber attacks, could spread unpredictably and disrupt the global economy, markets, asset values, currencies, trade, and confidence, causing borrower defaults and harming the firm’s operations and earnings. U.S. involvement could force JPMorgan Chase to curtail operations in affected or opposing countries and expose it to more aggressive adversary-sponsored cyber attacks.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s business and operations in certain countries can be adversely affected by local economic, political, regulatory and social factors.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces risks from volatile or government-controlled markets, economic crises, restrictive policies, and political or social unrest, which can disrupt local and cross-border operations, revenues, growth, and profitability. Its success also depends on attracting and retaining qualified, diverse employees and leaders; hybrid-work changes and immigration or travel restrictions may impair performance, controls, staffing, or efficiency. Litigation, investigations, examinations, and regulatory enforcement can result in penalties, restructuring, reputational harm, higher costs, and losses exceeding reserves.

nodes.title: Geopolitical and Workforce Risks
key_items: People JPMorgan Chase’s ability to attract and retain qualified and diverse employees is critical to its success.
Unfavorable changes in immigration or travel policies could adversely affect JPMorgan Chase’s businesses and operations.
nodes.summary: Geopolitical and social disruptions—including security threats, conflict, government overthrow, terrorism and internal discord—can harm JPMorgan Chase’s operations, revenues, growth and profitability across countries, including the U.S. The firm’s success depends on attracting, retaining and developing qualified, diverse employees and senior-leader successors; competition, recruitment by rivals and hybrid-work choices could weaken performance, controls or workforce retention. Restrictive immigration or travel policies could impede employee mobility and hiring, reduce workforce quality, or force less efficient or more costly operating models.

nodes.title: Legal JPMorgan Chase faces significant legal risks from litigation and formal and informal regulatory and government investigations.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces extensive litigation, regulatory scrutiny and overlapping U.S. and international investigations that may lead to sanctions, operational changes, reputational damage, higher costs, reduced profitability or losses exceeding reserves. It reports no unresolved staff comments; identifies its New York headquarters and ongoing replacement-building construction; refers material legal proceedings to Note 30; and states mine safety disclosures are not applicable. The text lists owned or leased facilities by region and square footage, including 4,787 branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C., and notes that excess-property disposals may be difficult or costly.

summary: JPMorgan Chase outlines non-exhaustive risks that could harm its business, financial condition, capital, liquidity, results or reputation. They include extensive and inconsistent regulation, enforcement, resolution and loss-absorbing requirements; political, economic, market, interest-rate, credit, collateral, liquidity, funding, ratings and benchmark-transition risks; operational, cyber, privacy, workforce, vendor, model, control and reporting failures; strategy, competition and climate risks; employee conduct, conflicts, fiduciary duties and reputational damage; geopolitical and country conditions; and litigation and government investigations. The section also discusses regulatory constraints on the parent and subsidiaries, workforce attraction and retention, and legal proceedings and property disclosures.

title: Part II
key_items: Repurchases under the common share repurchase program
summary: JPMorgan Chase’s common stock trades on the NYSE; the filing references stock-performance comparisons, dividends and restrictions, 203,141 record holders, and employee-plan securities. It describes the $30 billion repurchase authorization, temporary 2022 suspension and 2023 resumption, and 2022 repurchases and related amounts. Items 6–8 identify the MD&A, market-risk disclosures, financial statements, auditor’s report, and glossary. Item 9 reports no accounting disagreements. title: FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT

nodes.title: Risk governance framework
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase manages inherent business risks to balance client, customer and investor interests with the Firm’s safety and soundness. Its approach emphasizes individual accountability and escalation, business-unit ownership, firmwide oversight, and Board oversight of compensation, with risk and control issues considered in performance and incentives. The governance framework assesses risk drivers, four categories (strategic, credit and investment, market, and operational—including compliance, conduct, legal, estimation and model risk), and quantitative or qualitative impacts. Independent Risk Management, led by a Board-approved CRO, sets and oversees governance through Risk Management and Compliance leaders; LOB CROs oversee unit risks, while Firmwide Risk Executives address cross-unit, functional and regional risks. All areas must follow IRM parameters and their own risk and control standards.

nodes.title: Three lines of defense
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s three lines of defense: business and corporate units identify and manage risks through controls and compliance; Independent Risk Management (IRM) independently challenges them and develops policies; and Internal Audit independently assesses firmwide controls, governance, processes, and risk management, reporting to the Audit Committee and administratively to the CEO. Finance, HR, and Legal support the control environment outside these lines. LOBs and Corporate identify and catalog material risks, while IRM reviews, challenges, maintains the central repository, and reports consolidated results to the Firmwide Risk Committee and Board Risk Committee. Quantitative and qualitative risk appetite is periodically set by senior management, including the CEO and CRO, approved by the Board Risk Committee, monitored against risk capacity, and reported to that committee.

nodes.title: Risk Governance, Ownership and Appetite
nodes.summary: The page outlines the three lines of defense: business and corporate functions manage risks and follow IRM governance; IRM independently challenges risk practices and develops its own policies; Internal Audit objectively assesses firmwide controls and governance. Finance, HR and Legal also support controls and manage risks in their areas. LOBs and Corporate identify and control risks, while IRM reviews, challenges and consolidates them for risk committees and the Board. Senior management sets risk appetite for quantitative and qualitative risks, subject to Board Risk Committee approval; assessments monitor capacity and results are reported to the committee.

nodes.title: Risk governance and oversight structure

The Operating Committee, comprising the CEO, CRO, CFO, General Counsel, LOB CEOs, and other senior executives, is accountable to the Board, may refer matters to it, and must escalate information needed for the Board to perform its duties.

It also outlines senior management committees governing firmwide, business, regional, operational, asset-liability, and valuation risks, then lists the risk governance functions covered in subsequent sections, from strategic, capital, liquidity, credit, market, climate, and operational risks to compliance, conduct, legal, and model risks.

title: STRATEGIC RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: Strategic risk is the potential harm to earnings, capital, liquidity or reputation from flawed business plans or inadequate responses to changing conditions. The Operating Committee and LOB and Corporate leaders manage major strategic risks, with IRM participating in business decisions, reviews, governance forums, acquisitions and new initiatives. Management identifies initiative-related risks within the Firmwide Risk Identification framework and assesses effects on risk appetite; IRM also evaluates impacts on the Firm’s risk profile. The periodically reviewed strategic plan covers strategy, budget, risk appetite, capital, earnings and asset-liability objectives, and is informed by performance and the operating environment. The Board reviews and approves the plan, which is reflected in the budget. Balance-sheet strategy—focused on risk-adjusted returns, capital and liquidity—is also part of strategic risk management; related capital, liquidity and reputation risks are addressed elsewhere.

title: CAPITAL RISK MANAGEMENT

nodes.title: Capital Risk, Management and Governance
nodes.summary: The page explains capital risk and the Firm’s strategy of maintaining a strong, stable balance sheet through normal and stressed conditions, considering capital impacts before major decisions. An independent Capital Risk Management function oversees risk metrics, limits, breaches, capital-management activities and regulatory compliance. Treasury and CIO manage capital to support businesses and investments, strengthen subsidiaries, remain above regulatory requirements, meet distribution goals and fund resolution; they use internal minimums, flexibility, monitoring and escalation protocols. Capital oversight involves designated management committees and periodic Board Risk Committee review of capital risk tolerance.

nodes.title: Capital planning and stress testing
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve annually requires large bank holding companies to submit board-approved capital plans and uses CCAR and stress tests to assess capital adequacy, planning processes, and proposed distributions, including setting the Stress Capital Buffer. The Firm completed 2022 CCAR; its SCB rose from 3.2% to 4.0% and its standardized CET1 requirement, including buffers, rose from 11.2% to 12.0%, effective October 1, 2022 through September 30, 2023. The Firm’s annual ICAAP integrates stress testing and capital planning, informs the Board about capital management and supervisory compliance, and is reviewed under a framework approved by the Audit Committee. Scenarios apply centrally defined macroeconomic factors, global market shocks, and operational-risk events to assess vulnerabilities; management also uses tailored scenarios and sensitivity analyses.

nodes.title: Regulatory capital
Basel III Overview
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve sets capital requirements for the consolidated financial holding company, while the OCC sets similar standards for the Firm’s insured depository subsidiaries; U.S. rules generally follow Basel accords. Basel III sets minimum capital ratios and adequacy standards, with required capital based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) calculated under Standardized and Advanced approaches. The Firm is assessed against the more binding applicable approach; currently, Standardized ratios are more binding. Credit-risk RWA uses supervisory risk weights under Standardized and internal models under Advanced; market-risk RWA is calculated similarly, and Advanced also includes operational-risk RWA. Management judgment and regulatory feedback may supplement RWA. Advanced organizations must also calculate the supplementary leverage ratio (SLR).

nodes.title: Key Regulatory Developments CECL regulatory capital transition.
key_items: Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk
nodes.summary: The text describes two 2022 regulatory capital developments. The COVID-related CECL transition benefit began phasing out on January 1, 2022, at 25% annually over three years; at year-end, $2.2 billion of the original $2.9 billion CET1 benefit remained, and 25% of other CECL transition provisions affecting Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA was phased out. The Firm also adopted SA-CCR, replacing the Current Exposure Method for specified derivatives exposure and leverage calculations. Adoption increased Standardized RWA by about $40 billion, lowered the CET1 ratio by about 30 basis points, modestly reduced total leverage exposure, and increased Advanced RWA to a lesser extent.
