nodes.summary: The page describes U.S. broker-dealer and non-U.S. subsidiary capital requirements and December 31, 2022 positions. J.P. Morgan Securities’ net capital was $24.989 billion versus a $5.628 billion minimum; its swap-dealer tentative capital exceeded applicable minimum and notification thresholds. J.P. Morgan Securities plc and J.P. Morgan SE are subject to UK and EU Basel III, leverage, and MREL rules, respectively, and met MREL and applicable capital requirements. Tables show their capital ratios and regulatory minimums.

summary: Covers the Firm’s capital-risk strategy, governance, oversight, limits, and capital management in normal and stressed conditions; Federal Reserve capital planning, CCAR, stress testing, ICAAP, scenarios, and the contingency capital plan; U.S. Basel III rules, capital measures, requirements, buffers, surcharges, TLAC, eligible debt, and reported capital and leverage data; RWA rollforwards, SLR, and segment capital allocation; dividends, share repurchases, and preferred-stock actions; and regulatory capital requirements and positions of U.S. broker-dealers and non-U.S. subsidiaries.

title: LIQUIDITY RISK MANAGEMENT

nodes.title: Liquidity Risk Management, Funding and Governance
nodes.summary: Defines liquidity risk as inability to meet obligations or maintain suitable funding and liquidity. The independent Liquidity Risk Management function oversees risk metrics, limits, breaches, reviews, stress tests, positions and assumptions. Treasury and CIO manage liquidity to support businesses and obligations, optimize funding, analyze balance-sheet liquidity, set stress assumptions and strategies, manage limits and regulatory compliance, and set liquidity-based FTP. A centralized global approach optimizes sources and uses, monitors exposures and transfer constraints, and maintains surplus liquidity. Governance involves firmwide, business-line and regional committees, with the Board Risk Committee reviewing and recommending tolerances, strategy and policy for Board approval.

nodes.title: Internal stress testing
nodes.summary: The text describes the Firm’s regular and event-driven liquidity stress tests, their assumptions and use in funding plans, liquidity management across the Parent Company, IHC and subsidiaries, and its contingency funding plan. It explains LCR/HQLA requirements and methodology, reports average LCRs for the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. across three periods, and attributes recent declines to lower cash, deposits, loan growth and securities values. It also details other liquidity sources: unencumbered securities ($694 billion in 2022 versus $914 billion in 2021) and borrowing capacity at Federal Reserve Banks and FHLBs ($323 billion versus $308 billion), noting market dependence and that central-bank capacity is not a primary source.

nodes.title: Liquidity Risk Plans, LCR and Funding Sources
nodes.summary: The page describes the Firm’s contingency funding plan for liquidity stress, including limits, indicators, risk tolerances and alternative resources. It explains LCR requirements, HQLA eligibility and calculation, reports average LCR and excess HQLA for the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. across three periods, and attributes recent LCR declines to lower cash and securities, deposit declines and loan growth. It also covers unencumbered marketable securities and pledged-collateral borrowing capacity, their year-over-year changes, and why central-bank capacity is not considered a primary liquidity source.

nodes.title: NSFR
NSFR (intro)
nodes.summary: The NSFR is a liquidity requirement for large banks comparing available stable funding with required funding over a one-year horizon. As of December 31, 2022, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. met the 100% minimum under the Firm’s interpretation of the final rule. The Firm must begin semiannual public disclosures of its quarterly average NSFR in the second half of 2023.

nodes.title: Funding Sources of funds
nodes.summary: The Firm says its diversified secured and unsecured funding, deposits and equity cover short- and long-term obligations; excess funding is invested in securities or liquid assets. The text details funding by bank and non-bank subsidiaries and refers readers to Note 28 on off-balance-sheet obligations. It provides 2022 and 2021 period-end and average deposits by business line, explains deposits’ liquidity benefits and trends—including growth, attrition, spending and interest-rate effects—and notes deposit insurance protections and estimated uninsured balances of $1,383.7 billion in 2022 versus $1,489.6 billion in 2021.

nodes.title: Deposits
nodes.summary: Management says diversified deposits, secured and unsecured market funding, and equity adequately fund obligations; excess liquidity is invested or held in cash. The text presents 2022–2021 deposit balances by business, average deposit trends and causes of changes, deposit stability and insurance, uninsured deposit estimates and time-deposit maturities, loan-to-deposit ratios, and deposit balances and rates by account type and geography for 2022–2020. It also details nondeposit short- and long-term funding balances and averages, categories and references, and explains 2022 changes in secured financing, commercial paper, and funding fluctuations.

nodes.title: Funding Sources and Short-Term Funding
nodes.summary: Presents period-end and average 2022 and 2021 balances for funding excluding deposits, covering short- and long-term unsecured and secured funding, preferred stock, and common equity, with notes defining selected categories and cross-references. Explains that short-term secured funding is mainly securities loaned or repurchase agreements backed largely by high-quality securities; repo balances rose at year-end 2022 due to increased Markets trading-asset financing, partly offset by lower Treasury and CIO AFS financing. Unsecured funding mainly comprises commercial paper and other borrowings; commercial paper fell at year-end but average balances rose due to changes in issuance for liquidity management. Secured balances fluctuate with client activity, financing needs, liability-mix management, and market and portfolio factors.

nodes.title: Long-Term Funding and Issuance
nodes.summary: Long-term funding supports stable funding and liquidity, with plans shaped by client activity, liquidity, and regulatory requirements such as TLAC; objectives include diversification, market access, and cost optimization across markets, tenors, and currencies. Most unsecured debt is issued by the Parent Company, which passes proceeds to the IHC; the IHC issues no external debt. Tables report 2022 and 2021 unsecured issuance and maturities/redemptions by issuer and instrument, including TLAC-eligible structured debt. The Firm also raises secured long-term funding through credit-card loan securitizations and FHLB advances, with related issuance and maturities summarized.

nodes.title: Long-term secured funding
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021–2022 long-term secured funding issuance and maturities/redemptions by credit-card securitizations, FHLB advances and other secured funding, noting that client-driven loan securitizations are excluded because they are not Firm funding. It explains how credit-rating changes may affect financing, liquidity, collateral and commitments, while stating the Firm believes it can withstand downgrades. It lists 2022 ratings and outlooks for the parent and principal subsidiaries, notes Moody’s September upgrade of the parent, confirms unsecured debt has no rating-triggered acceleration or collateral provisions, and describes factors supporting ratings and those agencies monitor.

The section explains the NSFR requirement, the Firm’s compliance with the 100% minimum at year-end 2022, and upcoming disclosures. It describes funding sources and deposit balances, trends, stability, insurance and uninsured amounts, maturities, rates and loan-to-deposit ratios; short- and long-term secured and unsecured funding, balances, issuance, maturities and drivers; and long-term funding strategy, issuers, securitizations and FHLB advances. It also covers rating effects, current ratings and outlooks, protections against rating-triggered acceleration or collateral demands, and factors monitored by rating agencies.

summary: Defines liquidity risk and outlines independent oversight, Treasury/CIO responsibilities, centralized liquidity management, limits, stress assumptions, funding strategies, FTP, regulatory compliance and Board/committee governance. Covers regular and event-driven stress tests, contingency funding plans and liquidity across entities; LCR/HQLA requirements, methodology, trends and drivers; unencumbered securities and borrowing capacity, changes and limitations; and NSFR compliance. Describes deposits and their characteristics, secured and unsecured funding, issuance, maturities, long-term funding strategy, securitizations, FHLB advances, credit ratings, rating-trigger protections and agency monitoring.

title: REPUTATION RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: Reputation risk is the possibility that actions or inaction undermine perceptions of the Firm’s integrity or competence among stakeholders. The Firm’s governance function maintains its policy and standards and oversees processes and infrastructure for identifying, escalating, managing and monitoring risk across businesses and Corporate. Risks may arise from Firm employees or business partners and cause financial, legal, regulatory or other harm. Employees must consider reputation when evaluating products, transactions, relationships, jurisdictions, processes and other activities; environmental and social concerns are part of this assessment, and material issues are escalated as appropriate.

title: CREDIT AND INVESTMENT RISK MANAGEMENT
key_items: Credit risk management; Risk identification and measurement; Stress testing
Risk monitoring and management; Risk reporting
summary: The text outlines the Firm’s credit and investment risk, covering consumer, wholesale, and investment exposures. Credit Risk Management sets policies, authorities, limits, underwriting standards, and loss estimates. Credit is measured using default probability, loss severity, and exposure, with allowances and capital allocations reflecting expected and potential losses. Stress tests assess alternative economic, industry, and country scenarios. Monitoring includes portfolio trends, concentrations, risk ratings, distressed exposures, and independent model validation and Credit Review. Wholesale risks are mitigated through underwriting, syndication, sales, derivatives, netting, and collateral. Regular reporting informs senior management, committees, and the Board.

title: CREDIT PORTFOLIO
key_items: Customer and client assistance; Paycheck Protection Program (“PPP”)
summary: Defines credit risk and explains the scope and related notes for reported loans and other credit exposures. Presents 2022 and 2021 credit portfolio components, collateral and credit-management offsets, nonperforming assets, nonaccrual-loan ratios, and net charge-offs and rates, with qualifications for government-insured mortgages, credit cards, and SBA-guaranteed PPP loans. Describes pandemic-related customer assistance and its potential to delay delinquency and loss recognition, and summarizes PPP terms, expiration, outstanding balances by business segment, and past-due exclusions.

title: CONSUMER CREDIT PORTFOLIO
key_items: Maturities and sensitivity to changes in interest rates
summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s retained consumer portfolio, focused mainly on prime borrowers, including residential mortgages, credit cards, auto and business banking loans, and commitments; it explains loan retention, securitization and sales. Tables compare 2022 and 2021 exposures, balances, nonaccrual loans, charge-offs, average loans and loss rates across consumer categories, with notes defining exclusions, guarantees, commitments and credit protection. A second table presents 2022 consumer loan maturities and fixed-versus-variable interest-rate distribution, based on a revised scheduled-repayment methodology, with related qualifications.

title: Consumer, excluding credit card Portfolio analysis
key_items: Geographic composition and current estimated loan-to-value ratio of residential real estate loans
Nonperforming assets; Nonaccrual loans; Purchased credit deteriorated (“PCD”) loans
summary: Consumer loans excluding credit cards declined in 2022, as lower residential loans at fair value and auto/other balances outweighed growth in retained mortgages. The text reviews residential mortgage portfolio trends, credit performance, HELOC and interest-only loan balances and risk controls, government-insured loans, geographic concentration and LTVs, and modified loans. Auto and other balances, charge-offs, and rates are discussed. Tables report nonperforming assets and exclusions, nonaccrual-loan activity, and PCD loan delinquency, nonaccrual, and loss data; Note 12 is cited for further credit-quality details.

title: Credit card
key_items: Geographic and FICO composition of credit card loans; Modifications of credit card loans
Geographic and FICO composition of credit card loans
summary: Credit card loans grew in 2022 due to higher consumer spending and new originations. Delinquency rates rose from 2021 but remained below pre-pandemic levels, while net charge-offs declined; results continued to benefit from U.S. consumer financial strength, although median deposits fell in the second half as spending increased. Loans generally remain on accrual until charged off, with the allowance covering estimated uncollectible accrued and billed interest and fees. Five states held $85.4 billion (46%) of retained loans, versus $70.5 billion (46%) in 2021. Modified TDR loans totaled $796 million, down from $1.0 billion; short-term or insignificant modifications are excluded. Note 12 provides further portfolio details.

title: WHOLESALE CREDIT PORTFOLIO

nodes.title: Wholesale credit portfolio
nodes.summary: The section describes wholesale credit risks arising from client and counterparty activities, operating services, securities financing, and bank deposits. The Firm retains some originated loans, syndicates others, and actively monitors credit quality, structures, collateral, and concentrations; the portfolio spans CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate, and certain CCB exposures. In 2022, performance remained strong with low charge-offs. Retained loans rose $43.3 billion, while lending commitments fell $14.5 billion. Investment-grade exposure stayed near 70%; criticized exposure declined $6.9 billion to $31.3 billion, and nonperforming exposure fell $406 million. The table details 2022 and 2021 credit exposures, portfolio assets, commitments, and risk-management offsets from credit protection and collateral. Notes explain customer receivables, credit derivatives, and revised prior-period presentation.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – maturity and ratings profile
nodes.summary: Presents wholesale credit portfolio maturity and internal ratings profiles at December 31, 2022 and 2021, with exposure categories, totals, investment-grade/noninvestment-grade amounts, and investment-grade percentages. The Firm generally defines investment grade as ratings equivalent to BBB-/Baa3 or higher and considers collateral and structural support. Notes explain loans held for sale, credit derivatives and credit-related notes, ratings methodology, revisions to prior-period presentation, and contractual-maturity assumptions and caveats for derivative receivables.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industry exposures
nodes.summary: The Firm manages and diversifies wholesale credit exposures, with particular attention to industries facing actual or potential credit concerns. Criticized exposures follow U.S. banking regulator categories (special mention, substandard and doubtful). Excluding loans held for sale and at fair value, these exposures fell from $38.2 billion (3.5% of total wholesale credit exposure) in 2021 to $31.3 billion (2.7%) in 2022, due to net portfolio activity and client upgrades—especially in Consumer & Retail, Technology, Media & Telecommunications, and Real Estate—largely offset by downgrades. About half of 2022 criticized exposure was undrawn, and $28.6 billion was performing. The text introduces an industry breakdown of exposures for both years, generally classified by clients’ or counterparties’ primary business activity, with further information in Note 4.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industries (a)
nodes.summary: The text reports JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale credit exposure by industry for 2022 and 2021, with credit-quality categories, past-due loans, charge-offs or recoveries, credit-derivative hedges, collateral, and totals, plus explanatory definitions and scope notes. It then details real estate exposure: 2022 and 2021 balances by property type, lending commitments and derivative receivables, investment-grade and drawn percentages, changes in criticized exposure, and notes on multifamily geography, property classifications, and secured exposure.

nodes.title: Real Estate
nodes.summary: The discussion reports real estate exposure of $170.9 billion at December 31, 2022, with criticized exposure down $1.2 billion year over year to $4.0 billion, as upgrades and portfolio activity were largely offset by downgrades. A table compares 2022 and 2021 exposure by property type, showing loans and lending-related commitments, derivative receivables, total credit exposure, investment-grade percentages, and drawn percentages. Multifamily exposure is largely in California; other income-producing properties include diversified or uncategorized property types. About 79% of real estate exposure is secured, and unsecured exposure is approximately 77% investment-grade; drawn exposure is measured as a share of credit exposure.

nodes.title: Consumer & Retail
nodes.summary: Consumer & Retail exposure was $120.6 billion at year-end 2022, down from $122.8 billion in 2021; criticized exposure fell $1.9 billion to $7.9 billion, mainly from portfolio activity and upgrades, partly offset by downgrades. Tables detail 2022 and 2021 lending commitments, derivative receivables, credit exposure, investment-grade shares and drawn ratios across subsectors. Retail and Leisure categories are defined; 90% of non-investment-grade Leisure exposure is secured, and overall exposure is 58% secured, with 80% of unsecured exposure investment-grade. Oil & Gas exposure was $38.7 billion, down from $42.6 billion; criticized exposure fell $1.2 billion to $505 million for similar reasons. Tables provide the same metrics for E&P/oilfield services and other Oil & Gas. Other Oil & Gas categories are defined; 41% of exposure is secured, over half via E&P reserve-based lending, while 61% of unsecured exposure is investment-grade.

nodes.title: Oil & Gas
nodes.summary: The text reports 2022 and 2021 credit exposure by sub-sector for Consumer & Retail and Oil & Gas, including loans and lending-related commitments, derivative receivables, investment-grade and drawn percentages, and details on secured exposure. Criticized exposures declined in both sectors, with the stated portfolio and client upgrade/downgrade drivers. It defines included sub-sectors and notes that wholesale lending serves varied clients. Wholesale nonaccrual loans fell $50 million in 2022 to $2.395 billion, with activity shown by additions and reductions; net charge-offs were $181 million versus $142 million in 2021, with average loans, gross charge-offs and recoveries, and charge-off rates reported.

nodes.title: Wholesale Loan Credit Activity
nodes.summary: The page describes wholesale lending and refers readers to Note 12 for loan credit-quality details. It reports nonaccrual loan activity for 2022 and 2021: exposure fell $50 million in 2022 to $2.395 billion, mainly from client-specific upgrades and portfolio activity, partly offset by downgrades. It also presents average loans retained, gross charge-offs and recoveries, net charge-offs/(recoveries), and rates; sales-related gains or losses are excluded.

nodes.title: Maturities and sensitivity to changes in interest rates
nodes.summary: The text reports 2022 wholesale loan maturities and fixed/variable interest-rate distribution by loan class, noting a shift from contractual maturities to scheduled repayments, plus 2021–2022 net charge-offs, average retained loans, and charge-off rates. It explains wholesale lending commitments and why contractual totals do not represent expected exposure; customer margin receivables, collateral and risk controls; and derivative uses, counterparty risks, netting and collateral practices. It gives OTC collateral-agreement coverage and 2022/2021 derivative receivables, changes, collateral amounts, and net exposure.

nodes.title: Lending Commitments, Customer Receivables and Derivatives
nodes.summary: The page explains that lending commitments and guarantees represent maximum potential credit exposure but are usually not drawn. Customer margin loans are collateralized, monitored, and generally carry no credit-loss allowance. It describes derivative uses, counterparty risks, and mitigation through netting and collateral agreements (covering 87% of eligible OTC trades in 2022 versus 88% in 2021). Derivative receivables rose to $70.9 billion in 2022 from $57.1 billion in 2021, mainly due to foreign-exchange movements; tables show balances after cash collateral, liquid securities, and other collateral.

nodes.title: Derivative Receivables and Exposure Profiles
nodes.summary: The page reports 2021 and 2022 derivative receivables by investment-grade and noninvestment-grade ratings, as shares and amounts net of collateral. It explains Peak, DRE, and AVG measures of potential derivative credit exposure and their uses in limits, risk aggregation, pricing, capital, and CVA. It also describes counterparty credit valuation, active risk management, wrong-way risk adjustments, and hedging CVA changes. A graph profiles the three measures over ten years, generally showing exposure declining after year one if no trades are added.

nodes.title: Credit Derivatives and Portfolio Management
nodes.summary: The Firm uses credit derivatives as a market-maker and to manage its own credit exposures. Portfolio management derivatives mitigate risks from loans, lending commitments, and wholesale-business counterparty exposures; other securities-related hedges are excluded. The table reports net protection of $18.143 billion in 2022 versus $18.711 billion in 2021, split between lending exposures and derivative receivables. These derivatives are fair-valued without hedge accounting, while loans accrue, creating earnings volatility. CDS effectiveness can differ due to reference entities, contract terms, or maturities; the Firm generally aligns maturities and monitors differences.

summary: Covers wholesale credit risks and portfolio management across business segments, including 2022–2021 exposures, commitments, ratings, maturities, industries, collateral and credit-protection offsets. It details criticized, nonperforming and investment-grade exposures; industry profiles for real estate, consumer and retail, and oil and gas; nonaccrual loans, charge-offs, loan maturities and rate mix; customer receivables and lending commitments; derivative receivables, collateral, counterparty exposure measures and valuation risks; and credit-derivative hedging practices. Tables, definitions, methodology, scope and presentation notes are also discussed.

title: ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES
key_items: Discussion of changes in the allowance
Allocation of allowance for loan losses
summary: Defines the allowance for credit losses and its three balance-sheet components: loan losses, lending-related commitments, and investment securities. Explains the 2022 balance of $22.2 billion and $3.5 billion annual increase, driven by wholesale and consumer factors and revised macroeconomic outlooks; describes the five-scenario forecasting method, adverse-case projections, central-case unemployment and GDP assumptions for 2022 and 2021, and future estimate updates. Presents 2022 and 2021 allowance rollforwards and impairment methods by consumer, credit-card, and wholesale portfolios; retained-loan balances and credit ratios; relevant footnotes and references; and allowance allocations by loan class and each class’s share of retained loans.

title: INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: Investment portfolio risk covers potential principal losses or lower returns from securities and principal investments, generally held long term. Treasury and CIO securities totaled $629.3 billion at year-end 2022, with an average AA+ rating; credit risk is mitigated by high quality, while liquidity and market risks are discussed elsewhere. Securities risk is governed by the Risk Appetite framework, committee and Board oversight, independent valuation controls, and approved risk limits. Principal investments include private junior-capital interests, tax-oriented investments, and strategic investments managed by business units; the Firm’s strategy includes supporting underserved communities and minority-owned businesses. Carrying values rose from $30.5 billion in 2021 to $37.0 billion in 2022: tax-oriented investments were $23.2 billion and $26.2 billion, respectively, and private equity, debt, and real assets were $7.3 billion and $10.8 billion. The latter includes stakes in C6 Bank and Viva Wallet. Principal-investment governance includes independent approvals and valuation reviews, monitored portfolio limits, and scenario-based stress testing.

title: MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
key_items: Measures used to capture market risk
Distribution of Daily Backtesting Gains and Losses
summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s market-risk definition, governance, responsibilities, measurement tools, limits, breach escalation and model limitations. It outlines market risks and relevant positions across CCB, CIB, CB, AWM and Corporate. It describes Risk Management and Regulatory VaR methodologies, assumptions, uses, limitations and differences; presents 2022–2021 VaR results and drivers, including nickel volatility and lower Corporate exposure; and explains daily backtesting, its interpretation, exceptions, and reported 2022 outcomes.

title: Other risk measures Stress testing
key_items: Non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange risk; Other sensitivity-based measures
summary: The text describes market-risk tools and governance: stress testing across hypothetical market rallies, sell-offs, tail events, asset classes, geographies, and idiosyncratic/basis risks; results, limits, oversight, model controls, management and board reporting, and use in CCAR and risk appetite. It defines profit-and-loss drawdowns. It explains structural interest-rate risk, its sources, governance, management through Treasury/CIO, and earnings-at-risk scenarios, assumptions, limitations, model updates, and 2022 versus 2021 sensitivities for U.S. and non-U.S. dollar rates. It also covers structural foreign-exchange exposures and hedging, and sensitivity measures for debt, equity, credit, and funding exposures, including impacts, scenarios, reported values, and accounting treatment.

title: COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s independent Country Risk Management function, its framework, responsibilities, exposure attribution and measurement methods, and the distinction from FFIEC reporting. It explains tailored country stress testing, regular exposure and limit monitoring, and separate reporting for some dependent jurisdictions. It presents the top 20 non-U.S. country exposures for 2022 versus 2021, with table categories and scope notes, and explains notable changes in Germany, the U.K. and Australia, plus Russia exposure and the transfer of certain client deposits in February 2023.

title: CLIMATE RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: Climate risk encompasses climate change impacts on the Firm’s clients, operations, and strategy, and may affect existing risk types. It includes physical risks—acute events such as floods and wildfires, and chronic shifts such as sea-level rise—and transition risks from policy, technology, consumer changes, and physical climate effects. A dedicated function sets the Firmwide framework, policies, metrics, scenarios, stress tests, and data and technology strategy, and supports integration into risk management. LOBs and Corporate identify and manage business-related risks and comply with applicable rules. Governance follows the Firm’s risk structure, with relevant groups integrating climate risk and reporting significant risks and initiatives to the Board Risk Committee.

title: OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
key_items: Operational Risk Governance; Operational Risk Identification; Operational Risk Measurement; Operational Risk Monitoring and testing
Management of Operational Risk; Operational Risk Reporting
Subcategories and examples of operational risks
Business and technology resillency risk; Payment fraud risk; Third-party outsourcing risk
summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s operational risk definition, governance, and CCOR framework for identifying, assessing, measuring, monitoring, testing, remediating, and reporting risks. It describes self-assessments, independent oversight, risk-capital and stress models, escalation and Board reporting, and risk categories. Examples include sanctions related to the Ukraine war; cybersecurity threats, controls, governance, response, and training; business and technology resilience; payment fraud; and third-party outsourcing oversight. It also notes insurance as a means of mitigating operational risk.

title: COMPLIANCE RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: Compliance risk is the risk of violating laws, regulations, conduct codes, or standards. Business lines and Corporate own and manage these risks, while the independent Operational Risk and Compliance Organization oversees, monitors, tests, and reports them; other functions oversee obligations in their areas. Risks span products, customer relationships, employee conduct, anti-money laundering, trading, market conduct, cross-border activity, and fiduciary duties. Governance is led by the Global CCO and risk executive under the CCOR Management Framework, with significant issues reported to Board committees. The Code of Conduct sets employee standards, requires prompt reporting of violations and periodic training and annual affirmation. A globally available, generally anonymous third-party hotline accepts reports; retaliation for good-faith reporting is prohibited, and the Audit Committee periodically receives program updates.

title: CONDUCT RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: Conduct risk is operational risk arising from employee actions or misconduct that may cause unfair customer outcomes, harm markets, employees or the Firm, or damage reputation. Each business line and Corporate is responsible for managing it in line with the Firm’s Principles and Code, which guide ethical and legally compliant conduct. The CCOR Management policy governs the Conduct Risk Program. A senior forum sets strategic direction, connects initiatives, identifies emerging risks, and reviews the Firmwide risk appetite assessment. Management spans the employee life cycle; business units and designated functions periodically assess risks, review relevant metrics and issues, and provide education.

title: LEGAL RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: Legal risk is operational risk arising from actual or alleged failures to meet legal obligations under applicable laws, agreements, and the Firm’s products and services. The global Legal function manages litigation, enforcement, reviews, investigations, disputes, contracts, product and business advice, legal interpretation and advocacy, and counsel to business lines, Corporate, and the Board. It selects and oversees outside counsel and advises the Conflicts Office on potentially conflicted wholesale transactions. The General Counsel reports to the CEO, serves on key risk and control committees, and, with Legal colleagues, reports significant matters to the Board and Audit Committee. Legal also advises committees and business units on reputation risk.

title: ESTIMATIONS AND MODEL RISK MANAGEMENT
summary: The text defines estimation and model risk as adverse consequences from incorrect or misused outputs. The Firm uses models and other estimates for valuation, risk, regulatory capital, stress testing, credit-loss allowances and business decisions; MRGR independently governs related policies. Users and developers own model risks and handle development, testing, approval referrals, ongoing monitoring and maintenance. Models are tiered by complexity, exposure and reliance, and MRGR reviews suitability, methods, assumptions and testing, approving new models and material changes before use. Exceptions may require interim risk controls. Market or economic shifts, including early COVID-19, can increase model uncertainty and the need for judgment. Further valuation information is referenced in the critical estimates section and Note 2.

title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its controls for managing significant accounting estimates and judgments, then reviews key estimates: credit-loss allowances, including forecast scenarios, influential economic variables, sensitivity examples and limitations; fair-value measurement, Level 3 inputs and valuation adjustments; annual goodwill testing, with no impairment identified in 2022; credit-card rewards liability, its growth and sensitivity to redemption and cost assumptions; income-tax estimates, deferred-tax asset realizability, uncertain tax positions and potential effects of reassessments; and litigation reserves, with further details referenced in the notes.

title: ACCOUNTING AND REPORTING DEVELOPMENTS
key_items: Summary of guidance; Effects on financial statements
summary: The text summarizes FASB standards adopted since January 1, 2021 and standards issued but not adopted as of December 31, 2022. Reference Rate Reform guidance provides optional contract, hedge-accounting, discounting-transition, and securities reclassification expedients; JPMorgan elected certain expedients beginning in 2020, with no material financial-statement impact, and the options were extended through December 31, 2024. The Portfolio Layer Method expands eligible hedged portfolios and permits an HTM-to-AFS transfer; adopted prospectively January 1, 2023, it supported transfer of about $7.0 billion of securities. Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures guidance removes TDR accounting requirements and adds loan-modification and charge-off disclosures; adopted January 1, 2023 using modified retrospective transition, it reduced the credit-loss allowance by about $600 million and increased after-tax retained earnings by about $450 million.

title: FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS

nodes.title: FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS (intro)
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase explains that its SEC filings and management communications may contain forward-looking statements expressing current expectations, identifiable by predictive language. These statements are inherently uncertain, actual results may differ materially, and listed risks are not exhaustive. Risks include economic, political, geopolitical, regulatory, policy, inflation, market, credit, reputation, sustainability, operational, technological, cyber, workforce, competition, product, expense, control, litigation, accounting, valuation, disaster and climate-related factors, plus risks detailed in the 2022 Form 10-K. Statements speak only when made; the Firm undertakes no update duty, though readers should consult later SEC filings.

nodes.title: Management’s report on internal control over financial reporting
Management’s report on internal control over financial reporting (intro)
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase management describes internal financial-reporting controls, their purpose and inherent limitations, and reports that its COSO 2013-based assessment found controls effective with no material weaknesses at December 31, 2022. CEO James Dimon and CFO Jeremy Barnum signed the report on February 21, 2023. PwC’s independent audit opines that the 2022 and 2021 consolidated financial statements and 2022 internal controls are fairly presented and effective, respectively; it notes a 2020 change in credit-loss accounting, outlines management and auditor responsibilities and PCAOB audit procedures, and reiterates control definitions and limitations.

nodes.title: Auditor’s Opinions and Audit Basis
key_items: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: PwC reports unqualified opinions that JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 and 2021 financial statements fairly present its financial position, and that its 2022 internal controls were effective. The report notes a 2020 change in accounting for certain credit losses. It outlines management’s and auditors’ responsibilities, auditor independence and PCAOB-compliant procedures supporting reasonable assurance. It defines internal control’s financial-reporting safeguards and explains limits: controls may not prevent or detect misstatements, and effectiveness may change over time.

nodes.title: Critical Audit Matters
key_items: Allowance for Loan Losses – Portfolio-based component of Wholesale Loan and Credit Card Loan Portfolios
Fair Value of Certain Level 3 Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: The auditor explains that critical audit matters are material, especially challenging or complex audit issues and do not modify the overall opinion or constitute separate opinions. Two matters are detailed: the $17.0 billion portfolio-based allowance for wholesale and credit card loan losses, involving economic forecasts, models, and subjective adjustments; and the fair value of certain Level 3 instruments, involving significant unobservable inputs. For each, the auditor describes control testing, evaluation of management’s methods, assumptions and data, and specialist involvement. The auditor has served since 1965; report dated February 21, 2023.

Management explains the purpose and inherent limitations of internal controls over financial reporting and reports that its COSO 2013-based assessment found them effective, with no material weaknesses, as of December 31, 2022; the CEO and CFO signed the report on February 21, 2023. PwC gives unqualified opinions on the 2022 and 2021 financial statements and 2022 internal controls, noting a 2020 credit-loss accounting change, management and auditor responsibilities, PCAOB audit procedures, and limits of controls. It also details two critical audit matters—the $17.0 billion loan-loss allowance and valuation of certain Level 3 instruments—including related audit work and specialist involvement; these matters do not alter the overall opinion.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Consolidated statements of income
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s consolidated income statements for the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020 report revenue by noninterest category, interest income and expense, net interest income, total net revenue, credit-loss provisions, noninterest expenses by category and in total, pretax income, income tax expense, net income, net income attributable to common stockholders, basic and diluted earnings per share, and weighted-average basic and diluted shares. Amounts are in millions except per-share data; the accompanying notes are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Consolidated statements of comprehensive income
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income report net income, after-tax other comprehensive income or loss by category (investment securities, translation adjustments, fair value hedges, cash flow hedges, defined benefit pension and OPEB plans, and DVA on fair value option liabilities), total other comprehensive income or loss, and comprehensive income for the years ended December 31, 2020–2022. The statements note that the accompanying financial-statement notes are integral.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Consolidated balance sheets
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated balance sheets compare assets, liabilities, and stockholders’ equity at December 31, 2022 and 2021, in millions, including fair-value amounts, pledged assets, loan-loss allowances, and share data. They report total assets and total liabilities and equity, note commitments and contingencies, and describe consolidated VIEs: their assets support their liabilities, beneficial-interest holders have no recourse to the Firm’s general credit, and summarized VIE assets and liabilities are provided for both years. Financial-statement notes are integral.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders’ equity
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated statements of changes in stockholders’ equity present 2020–2022 annual balances and movements in preferred and common stock, additional paid-in capital, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive income or loss, restricted-stock-unit trust shares, and treasury stock. Changes include issuances, redemptions, employee share-based compensation, accounting changes, net income, dividends, other comprehensive income or loss, repurchases, and reissuances. Total equity was $279.354 billion in 2020, $294.127 billion in 2021, and $292.332 billion in 2022. The Firm adopted CECL on January 1, 2020; the notes are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Consolidated statements of cash flows
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated cash flow statements for 2020–2022 report operating, investing, and financing cash flows, including net income and adjustments, loan and securities activity, changes in deposits and borrowings, equity transactions, dividends, and other items. They also show foreign-exchange effects, net changes and beginning/end balances of cash and bank deposits, and cash interest and income taxes paid. The statements note that accompanying financial statement notes are integral.

They cover recognition of interest, customer-contract and fair-value revenue; estimates; foreign-currency translation; balance-sheet offsetting and master netting/collateral agreements; and the cash-flow definition of cash. They summarize 2023 troubled-debt-restructuring guidance and its allowance and retained-earnings effects, 2020 CECL adoption, and provide a cross-reference list of other significant accounting policies.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Fair value measurement
Valuation process
nodes.summary: JPMorgan measures some assets, liabilities, and lending commitments at fair value, recurring or in specific nonrecurring circumstances. Fair value reflects an orderly market-participant transaction and uses quoted prices or models with observable and unobservable inputs; methods involve judgment and may produce different estimates. Risk-taking functions estimate values, while independent Valuation Control verifies them and sets adjustments under senior governance oversight. Verification uses independent market data and additional reviews for harder-to-price positions. Adjustments may address liquidity, large net open positions, uncertainty in unobservable inputs, counterparty and own credit risk (CVA/DVA), and funding (FVA); Level 1 quoted prices are not adjusted.

nodes.title: Valuation model review and approval
nodes.summary: When instrument prices or comparable quotes are unavailable, fair value is generally estimated with models using transaction terms and market-based or independently sourced inputs; the usual price-verification process applies to those inputs. Under Firm policy, MRGR reviews and approves new models and material changes before operational use. Exceptions may permit interim use before approval, with MRGR potentially requiring risk-mitigating measures such as limits on trading activity.

nodes.title: Fair value hierarchy
nodes.summary: The text defines the U.S. GAAP fair value hierarchy: Level 1 uses unadjusted quoted prices for identical items in active markets, Level 2 uses observable inputs, and Level 3 uses significant unobservable inputs; classification follows the lowest significant input. It outlines valuation methods and typical hierarchy levels for securities financing, wholesale and consumer loans, securities, commodities, derivatives, mortgage servicing rights, private equity and fund investments, VIE interests, and structured notes. Methods include quoted or comparable prices, broker quotes, discounted cash flows, models, NAV, underlying-asset values, and adjustments for credit, funding, liquidity, and contractual features. It also introduces tables of assets and liabilities at fair value by product and hierarchy for 2022 and 2021.

nodes.title: Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s recurring fair-value assets and liabilities at December 31, 2022 and 2021, by instrument and fair-value hierarchy level (Levels 1–3), including derivative netting adjustments and totals. Categories include cash-equivalent agreements, trading and available-for-sale securities, loans, servicing rights, other assets, deposits, borrowings, trading liabilities, and other obligations. Notes explain mortgage-related GSE holdings, commodity inventory valuation, offsetting long and short securities, investments using NAV practical expedients, mortgage-loan balances and types, and derivative and collateral netting under enforceable agreements.

nodes.title: Level 3 valuations
nodes.summary: The Firm describes its Level 3 fair-value process: management selects valuation methods and uses judgment to derive significant unobservable inputs from empirical evidence; Level 3 instruments may also contain observable components, whose risks are managed with Level 1/2 positions. The 2022 table reports primary instruments, fair values, techniques, unobservable inputs, ranges and averages, with scope and calculation caveats. It covers mortgage securities and loans, debt, derivatives, mortgage servicing rights, structured funding and other assets/liabilities, and notes that input ranges reflect portfolio characteristics—not uncertainty or estimate reasonableness—and can change over time.

nodes.title: Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.summary: Explains how changes in unobservable valuation inputs affect fair value, noting that inputs may interact, observable–unobservable relationships are excluded, and inverse relationships generally apply. Describes yield and credit spreads, prepayment speeds, conditional default rates, loss severity, correlation, volatility, Bermudan swaption switch value, interest-rate curves, and forward prices: their meanings, key drivers and relationships, and the isolated direction of fair-value effects where specified. Input ranges reflect instrument characteristics, collateral and borrower quality, market conditions, risk type, tenor, and option terms.

nodes.title: Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.summary: Presents 2020–2022 rollforwards of Level 3 fair-value assets and liabilities, including opening and closing balances, gains/losses, purchases, sales, issuances, settlements, and transfers, across trading and other financial instrument categories. Explains Level 3 classification, observable inputs within measurements, and that results exclude risk-management instruments classified in Levels 1 and 2. Notes Level 3 shares of total fair-value assets and liabilities; derivatives are net; disclosures identify income-statement/OCI reporting, immaterial AFS and DVA amounts, loan originations in purchases, and items included in settlements.

nodes.title: Derivative Credit, Funding, and Liability Valuation Adjustments
key_items: Valuation adjustments on fair value option elected liabilities
nodes.summary: Explains how derivative fair values are adjusted for counterparty credit risk (CVA), funding costs and the Firm’s own credit risk (FVA/DVA), including key estimation inputs, collateral treatment, and the reported 2020–2022 revenue impacts excluding associated hedges. It also describes DVA on fair-value-option liabilities, based on changes in default probability and loss given default inferred from bond spreads, and where realized and unrealized gains or losses are reported.

nodes.title: Nonrecurring Fair Value Measurements and Changes
key_items: Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis
nodes.summary: Presents 2022 and 2021 nonrecurring fair-value assets and liabilities by product category and hierarchy level, with notes on equity securities valued using the measurement alternative and collateral-dependent residential loans, including valuation methods and discounts. Reports fair-value gains and losses for loans, other assets, and liabilities for 2022–2020, identifying measurement-alternative effects, and refers readers to Note 12 for collateral-dependent loan details.

nodes.title: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
nodes.summary: The Firm measures certain equity securities without readily determinable fair values using the measurement alternative: cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes, with changes recorded in other income and possible valuation adjustments. The text reports 2022 and 2021 carrying values and upward/downward changes, plus cumulative changes since 2018. It also describes Visa Class B shares, including the 2022 sale and gain, related conversion-rate derivative terms and accounting, shares sold and retained, a reported conversion-rate decrease, and uncertainty from litigation and transfer restrictions; Visa B shares remain at nominal value because they are not considered similar to Visa A shares.

nodes.summary: The disclosure explains U.S. GAAP fair-value reporting for financial instruments not carried at fair value, noting that the table excludes nonfinancial and other assets whose aggregate value management considers significant. It identifies short-term instruments whose carrying values approximate fair value and presents carrying and estimated fair values by hierarchy level for financial assets and liabilities at December 31, 2022 and 2021. Loan valuation methods, key assumptions, carrying-value differences, and revised comparative presentation are described. It also reports fair values of wholesale lending commitments, exclusions from those amounts, and why consumer off-balance-sheet commitments are not valued.

Note 3 – Fair value option (intro)
nodes.summary: The fair value option allows fair value measurement for selected financial assets, liabilities, firm commitments and written loan commitments. The Firm elects it to reduce income statement volatility from mismatched measurement bases and to reflect instruments managed at fair value. Elections cover certain loans and lending commitments, securities financing agreements, securitized-asset interests with embedded credit derivatives, structured notes and other hybrid instruments from client activities, and certain long-term interests in CIB consolidated securitization trusts whose underlying assets are at fair value.

title: Note 5 – Derivative instruments

summary: JPMorgan Chase uses derivatives mainly for client market-making and managing its own risks, offsetting client exposures with other contracts or instruments. Risk-management derivatives address interest-rate, foreign-exchange, commodity-inventory, and lending-related credit risks, including CDS. The text describes bilateral OTC, exchange-traded, and centrally cleared contracts, and client clearing services, whose contracts are excluded from the Firm’s financial statements. Own-account derivatives are recorded at fair value; qualifying netting agreements allow balance-sheet offsetting, while non-hedge derivatives’ fair-value changes go through earnings. Hedge accounting requires documented objectives and at least quarterly effectiveness assessment; ineffective hedges are discontinued. Fair-value, cash-flow, and net-investment hedge designations have distinct earnings, OCI, and termination treatments.

Tables compare 2022 and 2021 gross, netted, and net receivables and payables by contract type and settlement method, including balance-sheet totals, non-nettable collateral, and net amounts. It explains derivatives used in market-making and other activities, including managing open-position and counterparty risks, with gains and losses mainly in principal transactions revenue.
