key_items: Interest income; Nonaccrual loans; Allowance for loan losses
nodes.summary: The note explains loan accounting by category: held-for-investment loans are carried at amortized cost, with interest recognition, nonaccrual and return-to-accrual rules, expected-loss allowances, and consumer and wholesale charge-off policies, including collateral valuation methods. Held-for-sale loans are measured at lower of cost or fair value; fair-value-option loans are measured at fair value, with related income, fees, costs, and losses treated accordingly. It also describes transfers between portfolios and accounting for credit versus noncredit losses.

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase modifies loans for financially distressed borrowers to reduce losses and avoid repossession, offering concessions such as lower rates, extended terms, delayed payments, principal forgiveness, or assets instead of payments. Concessionary modifications are TDRs; insignificant changes are not. TDR loans other than credit cards are generally nonaccrual, but may return to accrual after at least six months or six payments of performance and when repayment is reasonably assured; limited current loans may remain accruing. TDRs are generally assessed using an asset-specific allowance that reflects expected redefaults and applies for the loan’s remaining life. Foreclosed property, including real, commercial, and personal assets, is recognized when received in satisfaction of debt, generally at foreclosure sale or deed-in-lieu. It is reported in other assets at fair value less selling costs, reviewed quarterly and written down to the lower of cost or fair value; valuation changes affect noninterest revenue, while operating costs are charged to other expense.

nodes.title: Loan portfolio
nodes.summary: The notes describe the Firm’s loan portfolio segments—Consumer excluding credit card, Credit card, and Wholesale—and the loan classes monitored for credit risk, including relevant scope and classification footnotes. Tables present balances by segment and accounting category (retained, held-for-sale, and fair value) at December 31, 2022 and 2021, with notes on accrued interest, write-offs, and loan discounts and fees. Additional tables report retained-loan purchases, sales, and reclassifications to held-for-sale in 2022 and 2021; later sales of reclassified loans are excluded.

nodes.title: Credit card
key_items: Gains and losses on sales of loans
nodes.summary: The notes describe the Firm’s three loan portfolio segments—Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card and Wholesale—and the loan classes monitored for credit risk, including relevant scope definitions. They present 2021–2022 balances by segment and accounting category, excluding accrued interest and noting loan carrying-value adjustments. Tables report retained-loan purchases, sales and reclassifications to held-for-sale for 2020–2022, with explanations of noncash reclassifications, mortgage repurchases and excluded correspondent-channel purchases. The section also reports loan-sale gains and losses and notes related allowance effects.

summary: Explains loan accounting by category, including interest recognition, credit-loss allowances, charge-offs, collateral valuation, portfolio transfers, and treatment of losses. Covers distressed-borrower modifications and troubled debt restructurings, accrual status, allowances, and accounting for foreclosed property. Describes portfolio segments and credit-risk loan classes, with balances by accounting category, accrued-interest and carrying-value details, purchases, sales and reclassifications, and loan-sale gains, losses, and related allowance effects.

title: Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio (intro)
nodes.summary: The notes describe consumer loans excluding credit cards, mainly scored prime residential mortgages, home equity, auto, and business banking loans, including junior-lien, interest-only, and payment-option loans that may negatively amortize. Retained balances totaled $300.8 billion in 2022 versus $295.6 billion in 2021; residential real estate was $237.6 billion and auto/other $63.2 billion in 2022. Auto/other included PPP loans of $350 million in 2022 versus $5.4 billion in 2021. Delinquency rates indicate credit quality, with over-30-day delinquencies an early warning and residential delinquencies over 150 days signaling likely liquidation. Other indicators include residential current LTV or combined LTV, collateral geography, and refreshed FICO scores; high LTV and low FICO imply greater risk. For scored auto and business banking loans, geography reflects regional economic conditions and events.

nodes.title: Residential real estate
nodes.summary: The text presents retained residential real estate loan credit-quality data at December 31, 2022 and 2021: delinquency by term-loan origination year and revolving-loan status, total balances, and 30+-day delinquency ratios. It explains government-insured-loan exclusions, treatment of COVID-19 deferrals and purchased loans, revolving-loan lien positions, and higher delinquency among converted loans. It also reports nonaccrual balances, loan distributions by estimated LTV and refreshed FICO bands, weighted-average LTV/FICO, and geographic balances, with methodology and accounting disclosures concerning collateral-dependent loans, Chapter 7 loans, interest income, valuation, and credit scores.

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.summary: Residential real estate loan modifications granted as concessions to financially distressed borrowers are generally TDRs; short-term or insignificant changes are excluded. New TDR carrying values were $362 million in 2022, $866 million in 2021 and $819 million in 2020, with no further lending commitments. Programs offer rate reductions, term/payment extensions, deferred payments, forgiveness or other concessions; the text reports trial and permanent modification counts and concession percentages for 2020–2022. It also reports permanent-modification interest rates, terms, charge-offs, deferred and forgiven principal, and one-year redefaults, defining default and noting likely liquidation and limitations in early redefault data. Modified TDRs had a six-year estimated remaining life at year-end 2022. Non-government-insured loans in active or suspended foreclosure totaled $565 million in 2022 and $619 million in 2021.

nodes.title: Auto and other
nodes.summary: Tables report retained auto and other consumer loan delinquency by origination year and loan type at December 31, 2022 and 2021, including current, 30–119-day and 120+-day past-due balances and delinquency ratios. Footnotes explain exclusions and treatment of SBA-guaranteed PPP loans and a revised prior-period figure. A second table gives nonaccrual balances and retained loan balances by geographic region for both dates, with notes on PPP exclusions and guarantees, allowance and collateral-dependent loan accounting, immaterial cash-basis interest income, and region ordering.

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.summary: Certain auto and other loan modifications offering concessions to financially distressed borrowers qualify as troubled debt restructurings (TDRs); short-term or insignificant modifications without concessions do not. The impact of modifications and new TDRs was not material in 2020–2022, and additional lending commitments to borrowers with TDR-modified loans were not material at year-end 2021 or 2022.

summary: Covers consumer loans excluding credit cards—primarily scored residential mortgages, home equity, auto, and business banking loans, including specialized mortgage features—and balances, delinquency indicators, collateral and borrower credit measures, and geographic risk. Residential real estate disclosures detail delinquency by origination year and loan status, nonaccruals, LTV/FICO distributions, geography, and related accounting methods and exclusions. They also report financially distressed-borrower modifications, concessions, redefaults, foreclosure balances, and remaining loan life. Auto and other disclosures present delinquency, nonaccrual balances, regional exposure, PPP/SBA treatment, and accounting notes; their TDR modifications were not material.

title: Credit card loan portfolio
key_items: Other credit quality indicators; Loan modifications
summary: The notes describe credit card portfolio credit-quality measures: delinquency is primary, geography provides economic context, and refreshed FICO scores offer a lagging, incomplete trend indicator; the Firm generally lends to prime borrowers. Tables report 2021–2022 retained-loan delinquency by revolving and converted-to-term status, geographic balances, and FICO distributions. They explain long-term hardship modifications (usually 60-month fixed-payment plans with reduced rates and treated as TDRs), treatment of nonconcessional modifications and noncompliance, and the financial effects of 2020–2022 TDRs, interest-rate reductions, and one-year redefaults. Payment default means two consecutive missed payments; modified loans remain in the program and follow standard charge-off policy.

title: Wholesale loan portfolio
summary: The notes describe wholesale loan credit-risk ratings, based on probability of default and loss given default, management’s rating factors, investment-grade and criticized classifications, and ongoing reviews. Tables report 2022 and 2021 retained loans by rating, loan class, origination year and revolving status, with PPP and other-loan definitions and exclusions. Additional disclosures cover real-estate loan types and construction lending, geographic distribution, delinquency and nonaccrual balances and allowance treatment. Loan modifications classified as TDRs, their forms, annual amounts, immaterial impact, and year-end carrying values are also presented.

title: Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses

nodes.title: Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lending-related commitments
nodes.summary: Note 13 describes the Firm’s allowance for credit losses, its components and financial-statement treatment, quarterly senior review, and the judgment and uncertainty involved. It explains expected-life estimates, treatment of cancellable commitments and accrued interest, and recovery expectations. Allowances are assessed collectively for exposures sharing consumer or wholesale risk characteristics, or individually for specified loans. Portfolio estimates use credit-risk models, five economic scenarios, forecasts, and management adjustments; individual estimates use expected cash flows or collateral values and account for loan modifications, potential redefault, and highly judgmental economic and borrower assumptions.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses and related information
key_items: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.summary: The notes present 2022, 2021 and 2020 allowances for loan losses and lending-related commitments, total credit-loss allowances, and loans and commitments by portfolio segment and impairment methodology. Footnotes explain CECL adoption, exclusions, asset-specific classifications, reporting location and commitment amounts outside the allowance. The discussion reports the 2022 allowance increase and its wholesale and consumer drivers, including macroeconomic and pandemic-related factors; describes the five-scenario estimation approach and adverse-scenario outcomes; lists central-case unemployment and GDP forecasts for 2022 and 2021; and notes future forecast effects and references further accounting and portfolio disclosures.

summary: Explains the Firm’s allowance for credit losses, its components, financial-statement treatment, quarterly senior review, and estimation uncertainty. Describes collective and individual assessment methods, expected-life estimates, cancellable commitments, accrued interest, recoveries, credit-risk models, five economic scenarios, management adjustments, and cash-flow or collateral-based estimates that consider modifications and redefault. Presents 2020–2022 allowance and portfolio data, classifications and reporting footnotes, the 2022 increase and its drivers, scenario outcomes, central-case economic forecasts, and expected forecast effects.

title: Note 14 – Variable interest entities

nodes.title: Significant Firm-sponsored variable interest entities
Credit card securitizations
nodes.summary: The note outlines JPMorgan Chase’s VIE consolidation policies and major Firm-sponsored VIEs: CCB credit-card and mortgage securitizations; CIB mortgage, consumer-loan and commercial securitizations, multi-seller conduits, and municipal-bond vehicles. It describes other segments’ VIE involvement, including AWM fund management and possible consolidation, CB lending without control or consolidation, and Corporate, Treasury/CIO, and CIB investments or services generally without consolidation. For credit-card trusts, the Firm consolidates because servicing and other responsibilities give it power and potentially significant exposure to losses and benefits. Trust assets are reserved for trust investors, and agreements generally require a 5% minimum undivided interest. At year-end 2022/2021, interests were $6.1/$7.1 billion; average principal-receivable interests were 62%/57%; the Firm retained $1.5 billion in subordinated, but no senior, securities. These interests and retained securities are eliminated on consolidation.

nodes.title: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
key_items: Residential mortgage; Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s sponsored mortgage and other securitizations, its servicing, retained interests, continuing involvement, consolidation criteria and maximum loss exposure. Tables compare 2022 and 2021 principal amounts and assets of consolidated and nonconsolidated trusts, and the Firm’s interests; footnotes explain exclusions, ratings and investment-grade holdings. It outlines residential and commercial mortgage and consumer securitization roles, plus re-securitization activity, transfers, client-shared decision-making, nonconsolidation rationale, and nonconsolidated interests for 2020–2022.

nodes.title: Multi-seller conduits
nodes.summary: The text describes Firm-administered multi-seller conduits: their receivables-backed commercial-paper financing, seller-provided credit enhancements, JPMorgan liquidity and credit support, and the Firm’s consolidation rationale and exposures. It reports conduit paper holdings, purchase obligations, eliminated balances, and unfunded client commitments for 2022 and 2021. It also explains municipal tender option bond trusts, their floater and residual securities, customer versus non-customer structures, the Firm’s sponsor, remarketing and liquidity roles, immaterial floater holdings, and conditional liquidity-provider obligations.

nodes.title: Municipal bond vehicles
nodes.summary: The notes report interests in nonconsolidated re-securitization VIEs of $2.58 billion in 2022 and $1.947 billion in 2021, and no consolidation of U.S. government or Firm-sponsored private-label re-securitization VIEs. They describe multi-seller conduits’ financing, credit and liquidity protections, the Firm’s consolidation rationale and roles, eliminated commercial paper holdings and facilities, and unfunded commitments of $10.6 billion and $13.4 billion. They also explain municipal tender option bond structures, services and conditional liquidity support, and why the Firm consolidates non-customer trusts.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s VIE consolidation policies and significant sponsored VIEs across credit-card, mortgage and other securitizations, multi-seller conduits, and municipal-bond vehicles, as well as other businesses’ VIE activities. Covers consolidation criteria, servicing and other roles, retained interests, assets, exposures, maximum loss and commitments; compares 2022 and 2021 balances and interests; and explains trust structures, investor protections, credit and liquidity support, transfers, re-securitizations, nonconsolidation rationales, and the Firm’s responsibilities in customer and non-customer vehicles.

nodes.title: Consolidated VIE assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: Presents consolidated VIE assets and liabilities by program type for December 31, 2022 and 2021, including trading assets, loans, other assets, total assets, beneficial interests in VIE assets, other liabilities, and total liabilities. Notes cover residential mortgage securitizations; receivables and auto securitizations included in “Other”; balance-sheet classifications; assets used to settle VIE liabilities and exclusion of eliminated intercompany balances; limited recourse of beneficial-interest holders; and long-term beneficial interests of $2.1 billion in 2022 and $2.6 billion in 2021.

nodes.title: VIEs, Tax Credit Vehicles, TOB Trusts and Loan Securitizations
key_items: Tax credit vehicles; Customer municipal bond vehicles (TOB trusts)
nodes.summary: The notes describe third-party-sponsored VIE transactions conducted at arm’s length and generally not consolidated when the Firm lacks significant decision-making power or exposure. The Firm does not consolidate tax credit partnerships controlled by third parties; it reports related maximum loss exposures and risk-mitigation practices. It also does not consolidate customer TOB trusts, outlining liquidity-provider exposure, recourse arrangements, and VIE asset values. Loan securitizations support investor demand and liquidity; qualifying transfers are recorded as sales, with gains or losses reported in noninterest revenue.

nodes.title: Securitization activity
nodes.summary: Reports 2020–2022 securitization activity for assets in nonconsolidated, Firm-sponsored entities where sale accounting applied, including principal securitized and cash flows from loan-sale proceeds, servicing fees, and interests received, by residential and commercial/other categories. Notes exclusions and classifications, including re-securitizations, predominantly Level 2 assets, prime mortgages excluding U.S. GSEs and government agencies, and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans. Also provides weighted-average life and discount rates for newly originated retained interests in residential and commercial mortgages.

nodes.title: Loans and excess MSRs sold to U.S. government-sponsored enterprises and loans in securitization transactions pursuant to Ginnie Mae guidelines
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s nonrecourse sales of mortgage loans and excess MSRs, mainly to U.S. GSEs, and loan sales into Ginnie Mae securitizations. The Firm generally does not consolidate these vehicles, though it shares some credit risk; related indemnifications and excess-MSR impacts are covered in other notes. A table reports 2020–2022 loan carrying values, cash and securities proceeds, total proceeds, and gains or losses, with explanatory footnotes. It also explains options to repurchase delinquent government-guaranteed loans and reports 2021–2022 balances for repurchased or eligible loans, real estate owned, and foreclosed loans.

nodes.title: Loan delinquencies and liquidation losses
nodes.summary: The table reports, in millions, loan balances, 90-days-past-due amounts, and net liquidation losses or recoveries for nonconsolidated securitized assets in Firm-sponsored private-label entities where JPMorgan Chase had continuing involvement, as of or for 2022 and 2021. It covers residential mortgage loans (prime/Alt-A and option ARMs, subprime, and commercial and other), total securitized loans, and securitized assets. A note says prior-period figures were revised to match the current presentation.

summary: Explains JPMorgan Chase’s VIE consolidation policies and activities, including sponsored securitizations, conduits, municipal vehicles, tax-credit partnerships and customer transactions. Covers roles, retained interests, assets, liabilities, exposures, maximum losses, commitments, investor protections, support arrangements, transfers and reasons for nonconsolidation, with 2021–2022 comparisons. Reports consolidated VIE balances; securitization activity, cash flows and retained-interest terms; mortgage and Ginnie Mae loan sales, proceeds, gains or losses and repurchases; and delinquencies and liquidation losses for nonconsolidated securitized loans.

title: Note 15 – Goodwill and Mortgage servicing rights Goodwill
summary: The note explains goodwill recognition, allocation, annual impairment testing, valuation methods, risks, and balances and movements by segment for 2020–2022, including acquisitions and currency effects; no impairment was recorded. It describes mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), fair-value measurement using an option-adjusted spread model, interest-rate sensitivity and hedging, and presents 2020–2022 MSR activity, servicing and mortgage-fee income, serviced loans and advances, plus 2021–2022 valuation assumptions and adverse-change sensitivities.

title: Premises, Equipment and Deposits
summary: Note 16 explains that premises, equipment, leasehold improvements, and capitalized internal-use software are carried or amortized using straight-line methods over applicable useful lives or lease terms, with periodic impairment assessments. Note 17 presents 2022 and 2021 U.S. and non-U.S. deposit balances, including fair-value amounts and a prior-period presentation revision; reports time deposits at or above insured limits; and lists 2022 maturities of interest-bearing time deposits by year and office location.

title: Note 18 - Leases Firm as lessee
summary: Notes 18–19 describe JPMorgan Chase’s lessee and lessor accounting and liabilities. Lessee disclosures cover operating-lease terms, recognition and measurement, expense treatment, restrictions and non-lease components, 2022–2021 asset, liability, term, discount-rate, cash-flow and rental-expense figures, future payments and signed leases not yet commenced. Lessor disclosures explain auto and equipment lease income, depreciation, impairment and residual-value risk management, with asset balances, income, depreciation and future receipts for 2020–2022. Accounts payable and other liabilities are described and totaled for 2022 and 2021, including brokerage payables, other liabilities and credit-card rewards balances.

title: Note 20 – Long-term debt
summary: JPMorgan Chase’s long-term debt is issued mainly in U.S. dollars, at fixed and variable rates; certain indexed instruments are measured at fair value, with most valuation changes in earnings and DVA changes in OCI. The note presents 2022 and 2021 carrying values by maturity, entity and debt type, plus beneficial interests and weighted rates. It details secured and fair-value debt, zero-coupon notes, beneficial-interest classifications, callable debt, and scheduled maturities for 2023–2027. It also reports average rates before and after derivatives, subsidiary debt guarantees, and that unsecured debt has no specified rating- or financial-condition-triggered acceleration, borrowing limits, or collateral requirements.

title: Note 21 – Preferred stock
summary: JPMorgan Chase’s preferred-stock note describes its authorization of 200 million $1-par shares, priority over common stock in liquidation, and the outstanding non-cumulative series in 2022 and 2021. It tabulates shares, carrying values, issue dates, contractual and floating rates, earliest redemption dates, and dividends declared for 2020–2022, with notes on depositary shares, payment frequency, prorated initial dividends, and Series CC’s rate conversion. Each share has a $10,000 liquidation value and redemption price plus unpaid dividends; aggregate liquidation value was $27.7 billion in 2022. The note lists 2021–2022 series redemptions and explains redemption rights, capital-treatment-event provisions, and the requirement for Federal Reserve non-objection.

title: Note 22 – Common stock
summary: JPMorgan Chase was authorized to issue 9.0 billion $1-par common shares. The text reports 2020–2022 share issuance, treasury repurchases and reissuances, and year-end outstanding shares. A $30 billion repurchase authorization took effect in May 2022; buybacks were paused in the second half amid expected higher capital requirements and resumed in Q1 2023. It gives annual repurchase share counts and costs, notes Federal Reserve restrictions in 2020–2021, and explains that management controls timing and methods based on capital, regulatory, market and investment factors; the program has no price targets or timetable and may be suspended. About 58.9 million shares were reserved for employee and director plans at year-end 2022.

title: Note 23 – Earnings per share
summary: Note 23 explains JPMorgan Chase’s basic and diluted EPS methods. Basic EPS uses the two-class method, allocating earnings to common stock and participating unvested RSUs that receive nonforfeitable dividends. Diluted EPS includes potentially issuable shares and reports the more dilutive result under the two-class or treasury stock method; the two-class method was more dilutive in all years shown. The table reports 2022, 2021 and 2020 net income, preferred dividends, earnings allocated to participating securities, common-stockholder income, weighted-average basic and diluted shares, dilutive awards, and basic and diluted EPS.

title: Note 24 – Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
summary: Note 24 defines AOCI components: after-tax investment-security unrealized gains/losses, currency translation and related hedges, fair value and cash flow hedges, defined-benefit pension/OPEB plans, and DVA on liabilities elected at fair value. It provides component balances and annual changes for 2019–2022, including transferred AFS-to-HTM security amounts, and pre-tax, tax-effect, and after-tax OCI changes for 2020–2022. Notes explain income-statement reclassifications, cross-currency basis spreads, and a 2022 pension-settlement remeasurement that reduced pre-tax AOCI by $1.4 billion.

title: Note 25 – Income taxes

nodes.title: Income Taxes: Rates, Expense, and Earnings
key_items: Results from U.S. and non-U.S. earnings
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its tax accounting method, deferred taxes and valuation allowances, and the judgments involved in tax estimates and audits. The page reconciles statutory and effective tax rates for 2020–2022; details current and deferred tax expense by jurisdiction, audit-resolution effects, and tax impacts recorded in equity; reports U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income; and notes that 2022 global intangible low-tax income tax expense was not material.

nodes.title: Affordable Housing Credits and Deferred Taxes
nodes.summary: The page reports affordable-housing investment tax credits and benefits, related amortization, carrying values, and commitments for 2020–2022. It explains deferred-tax asset recognition and valuation allowances, presents the major deferred tax asset and liability categories and totals for 2021 and 2022, and details 2022 tax-attribute carryforwards, their expiration periods, and the sources of the valuation allowance.

nodes.title: Tax Benefits and Examination Status
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase reports unrecognized tax benefits of $5.0 billion, $4.6 billion and $4.3 billion for 2022–2020, including amounts that would reduce the effective tax rate if recognized. A reconciliation details annual increases and decreases; the balance could change by about $1.0 billion over the next 12 months. After-tax interest and penalties, and accrued related liabilities, are disclosed. The page also summarizes significant ongoing IRS, U.S. state and local, U.K. and other worldwide tax examinations and the periods and examination statuses.

summary: Describes tax accounting policies, estimates, audits, and reconciliations of statutory and effective tax rates, tax expense, pretax income, equity impacts, and global intangible low-tax income. Covers affordable-housing tax credits, investments and commitments; deferred-tax assets, liabilities, valuation allowances, and tax-attribute carryforwards. Reports unrecognized tax benefits, potential changes, interest and penalties, and the status and periods of significant U.S. and international tax examinations.

title: Note 26 – Restricted cash, other restricted assets and intercompany funds transfers
key_items: Restricted cash and other restricted assets; Intercompany funds transfers
Restricted cash and other restricted assets
summary: The note describes regulatory restrictions on JPMorgan Chase cash and assets, including OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, central-bank reserve, and broker-dealer requirements. Restricted cash totaled $26.8 billion in 2022 versus $19.7 billion in 2021, with amounts and balance-sheet classifications specified; other restricted assets included customer-related pledged cash and securities and securities restricted by customer activity. It also explains legal limits on bank lending to affiliates, covered-transaction collateral and capital caps, the roles and funding relationships of the Parent Company and IHC, dividend and credit restrictions, regulators’ authority to limit dividends, and approximately $34 billion of subsidiary dividend capacity without prior approval at January 1, 2023, supplemented by earnings.

title: Note 27 – Regulatory capital
summary: Note 27 describes Federal Reserve and OCC Basel III capital rules for JPMorgan Chase and its insured depository institutions (IDIs), including Standardized and Advanced risk-weighted approaches and minimum CET1, Tier 1, total capital, Tier 1 leverage and SLR requirements. It provides 2022 and 2021 required and well-capitalized thresholds, regulatory definitions, buffers, surcharges and exceptions. It explains the COVID-era CECL capital transition and phase-out, then reports 2022 and 2021 risk-based and leverage-based capital metrics for the holding company and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. under both approaches, noting both met requirements and were well-capitalized.

title: Note 28 – Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments

nodes.title: Note 28 – Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments (intro)
nodes.summary: Note 28 explains JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance-sheet lending commitments, guarantees, and other obligations, whose contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk but do not reflect expected exposure or funding needs because most expire, are changed, or are refinanced without a draw or default. The Firm maintains an allowance for expected losses on wholesale and certain consumer commitments and presents contractual amounts and carrying values for 2022 and 2021. Credit card and home-equity figures represent total available credit, which is not expected to be used simultaneously; the Firm may reduce or cancel card lines, typically closing accounts 60 or more days past due, and may reduce or close HELOCs after significant property-value declines or reduced borrower creditworthiness.

nodes.title: Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
nodes.summary: The table reports JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 and 2021 contractual amounts by remaining maturity and carrying values for lending-related commitments, guarantees, and other off-balance-sheet obligations. Categories include consumer and wholesale credit commitments, letters of credit, securities-lending indemnities, derivatives, unsettled resale/repurchase and securities-borrowing/lending agreements, loan-sale indemnifications, clearing-house guarantees, and other commitments. Footnotes explain category scope and U.S. concentration, risk participations and regulatory presentation, collateral held, clearing-house and investment commitments, bridge-financing markdowns, and how carrying values are measured.

nodes.title: Credit Commitments and Guarantees
key_items: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
nodes.summary: Describes unfunded credit commitments for working capital, corporate purposes, backstopping commercial paper and bond financings, clearing liquidity, and multipurpose facilities. Explains U.S. GAAP’s definition and accounting for guarantees, including initial fair-value recognition, amortization, and recognition of contingent obligations, and notes that contractual amounts and carrying values are tabulated. Defines standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees as conditional commitments supporting clients’ obligations in various financings, with amounts and carrying values summarized for 2022 and 2021.

nodes.title: Standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees and other letters of credit
key_items: Securities lending indemnifications; Derivatives qualifying as guarantees
nodes.summary: The text reports 2022 and 2021 amounts for standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees, and other letters of credit, including credit ratings, contractual amounts, allowances and guarantee liabilities, carrying values, and collateralized commitments; ratings use the Firm’s internal scale. It describes securities-lending indemnities, daily collateral monitoring and remedies for borrower default, plus indemnities on invested cash collateral. It explains guarantee-like derivatives, including written puts and stable value contracts, their purposes, terms, exposure, fair value, and hedging, and provides 2022/2021 notional, maximum exposure, and payable figures. The Firm also buys and sells credit protection.

nodes.title: Unsettled securities financing agreements
nodes.summary: The Firm enters into resale and securities-borrowed agreements, under which it advances cash and receives securities collateral at settlement, and repurchase and securities-loaned agreements, under which it receives cash and provides collateral. These commitments settle in the future, predominantly on regular-way terms, generally are not derivatives, and are not recorded on the consolidated balance sheets until settlement. See Note 11 for further discussion.

nodes.title: Loan sales- and securitization-related indemnifications
key_items: Mortgage repurchase liabillty; Private label securitizations
nodes.summary: The text describes indemnification and recourse obligations arising from loan sales and securitizations. For U.S. GSE mortgage sales, breached representations and warranties may require repurchase or indemnification. Private-label securitization repurchase demands are assessed separately in litigation reserves (see Note 30). Mortgage and commercial loan servicing may be nonrecourse, exposing the Firm mainly to temporary servicing advances, or recourse, sharing credit losses with loan owners. Recourse losses arise when foreclosure proceeds do not cover principal, interest, and property costs. Most Firm securitizations are nonrecourse, transferring future credit risk to securities purchasers; balances of recourse loans and related recorded liabilities are disclosed on page 277.

nodes.title: Other off-balance sheet arrangements
key_items: Indemnification agreements – general; Merchant charge-backs; Clearing Services – Client Credit Risk
Exchange & Clearing House Memberships; Sponsored member repo program
nodes.summary: The text describes off-balance-sheet risks and guarantees: tax-related investor indemnities and software/business-sale indemnities (with expected remote losses); merchant charge-backs, risk mitigants, valuation allowance, and processed volumes for 2020–2022; client clearing services, margin, default procedures, accounting, and remote expected losses; exchange and clearing-house member loss-sharing obligations; sponsored-member repo guarantees secured by collateral; and Parent Company guarantees of subsidiary obligations and debt. It also reports pledged assets and their uses, categories and 2021–2022 totals, and accepted collateral, including amounts permitted for use and amounts actually sold, repledged, delivered, or used.

summary: Note 28 covers JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance-sheet lending commitments, guarantees, and other obligations, including contractual amounts, carrying values, maturities, allowances, maximum potential credit risk, and limits on credit-line use. It details credit commitments and guarantee accounting; letters of credit, securities-lending indemnities, and guarantee-like derivatives; unsettled securities-financing agreements; loan-sale and securitization indemnifications and recourse; and other arrangements involving tax, merchant, clearing, exchange, repo, and parent-company guarantees. It also discusses collateral, pledged and accepted assets, risk mitigants, and related exposures and losses.

title: Note 30 – Litigation Contingencies
key_items: Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation; Interchange Litigation; Jeffrey Epstein Litigation
LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation.
summary: As of year-end 2022, JPMorgan Chase faced numerous civil lawsuits, investigations and regulatory matters across businesses and geographies. It estimated reasonably possible losses above reserves at $0–$1.2 billion, while noting substantial uncertainty and that actual losses could differ significantly. The filing describes material matters involving 1MDB, Amrapali, Nigeria, foreign exchange, interchange fees, Jeffrey Epstein, benchmark rates, securities lending and shareholder claims, including key rulings, settlements and pending actions. The Firm maintains reserves, reviews them quarterly and reported legal expense of $266 million in 2022, $426 million in 2021 and $1.1 billion in 2020. It intends to defend claims, but outcomes, timing, reputational effects and losses remain uncertain; matters could materially affect results, though other pending proceedings are not currently expected to materially harm consolidated financial condition.

title: Note 31 – International operations

nodes.title: Preferred Stock and Ranking
nodes.summary: As of the Form 10-K filing date, 18 preferred stock series are outstanding, represented by depositary shares. Six registered series—DD, EE, GG, JJ, LL, and MM—each have depositary shares representing 1/400 of a preferred share; these fully paid, nonassessable series are collectively called Listed Preferred Stock, with depositary share terms summarized elsewhere. They rank equally with parity-ranking preferred stock, senior to common and junior preferred stock, and subordinate to existing and future indebtedness for dividends and liquidation distributions.

nodes.title: Dividend Rights
nodes.summary: Listed Preferred Stock dividends are payable in cash at specified rates and dates only when declared, to record holders; they are noncumulative, so undeclared dividends are forfeited. Dividend priority rules require full payment or provision for the latest period before dividends on equal- or junior-ranking stock, with parity shortfalls distributed pro rata using current and, for cumulative parity stock, accumulated unpaid amounts. Until preferred dividends are fully covered, dividends and certain redemptions or acquisitions of junior or equal-ranking stock are restricted, subject to listed exceptions and ordinary-course market activities. Otherwise, the board may authorize distributions from legally available assets, in which preferred holders do not participate. The text defines junior, parity, and senior ranking and specifies dividend calculation, day-count, and rounding methods.

nodes.title: Rights Upon Liquidation
nodes.summary: Upon liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, each Listed Preferred Stock series receives $10,000 per share plus declared, unpaid dividends (excluding undeclared dividends) before junior stock; it has no claim to remaining assets afterward. If assets are insufficient, equal-ranking stockholders share ratably. Asset sales, mergers, and consolidations do not count as liquidation. As a holding company, subsidiary creditors may have priority over claims to subsidiary assets. Preferred holders rank behind the company’s debt and other non-equity claims and may be fully subordinated to U.S. government interests in insolvency proceedings.

nodes.title: Redemption
nodes.summary: JPMorgan may redeem each preferred-stock series on specified terms or, in whole only, after a capital-treatment event, at $10,000 per share ($25 per depositary share) plus declared unpaid dividends; regulatory approval may be required. The text defines qualifying capital-treatment events and details redemption notice, selection, effects, and limits, including restrictions when dividends are unpaid and no holder right to demand redemption. The stock has no preemptive or conversion rights; Computershare is depositary, transfer agent, and registrar. Voting is generally unavailable, with one vote per share where permitted; six unpaid quarterly dividends trigger two additional directors and specified preferred-holder voting rights.

nodes.title: Preferred Stock Redemption and Administrative Rights
nodes.summary: A capital treatment event may permit redemption when a post-issuance legal or regulatory development creates more than an insubstantial risk that the preferred stock will no longer qualify as additional Tier 1 capital. Redemption may require regulatory approval, with 30–60 days’ notice stating key redemption details; DTC-held shares may receive notice under DTC procedures. Holders cannot require redemption. Partial redemptions are selected pro rata or by lot; dividends and other rights end on the redemption date except the right to payment. If full dividends are unpaid, partial redemption and acquisitions are restricted, except equal-terms offers to all holders. The stock has no preemptive or conversion rights. Computershare is depositary, transfer agent, and registrar.

nodes.title: Voting Rights
nodes.summary: Listed Preferred Stock generally has no voting rights except as specified or required by law; when voting, each share has one vote, based on share count. After six unpaid quarterly dividends, holders and voting parity stock may elect two directors until four consecutive quarters of dividends are paid; the text sets out their removal, replacement, vacancy, and termination rules. Specified senior-stock issuances and adverse amendments require 66⅔% approval, subject to listed exceptions and series-specific voting. Redemption with funds irrevocably held suspends these votes. The board may issue additional shares; Delaware law and the charter provide separate-class voting rules for certain amendments. Dividend-arrears voting rights may trigger Federal Reserve bank-holding-company regulation, acquisition approvals, or notice requirements at stated ownership thresholds.

nodes.title: General
nodes.summary: The Alerian MLP Index ETNs due May 24, 2024 are described as subject to the 2001 Indenture between JPMorgan Chase and Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, which is incorporated by reference. Their issuance cap was reduced from 129 million notes ($2.456 billion) to 119 million ($2.265 billion) after 10 million were retired in 2015; all remaining notes were issued and outstanding at December 31, 2019. The ETNs track the Alerian MLP Index, are unsecured and unsubordinated, rank equally with similar obligations, provide no guaranteed principal repayment, and carry issuer credit risk.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s Alerian ETNs are Series E debt securities, not bank deposits or government-insured or bank-guaranteed obligations; “holders” means registered owners, and capitalized terms are defined elsewhere. Returns track an energy-MLP index calculated by S&P Dow Jones Indices with GKD Index Partners using float-adjusted market capitalization. Notes are U.S.-dollar denominated, with a $19.03661 minimum principal amount. Quarterly coupons equal reference distributions less a daily accrued 0.85% tracking fee; unpaid fee excesses carry forward as shortfalls, and no coupon is paid until distributions exceed accumulated fees. Interim coupon values are published daily, while actual payments occur quarterly in arrears, with the final coupon included in maturity settlement. Holders may request early repurchase weekly, subject to procedures and possible disruption-related changes.

nodes.title: Alerian ETN Index, Denominations, and Coupons
key_items: Coupon Payments and the Accrued Tracking Fee
nodes.summary: Defines holders as registered owners and points to definitions for capitalized terms. The ETN return tracks an energy MLP index calculated by S&P Dow Jones Indices with its sponsor using float-adjusted market capitalization. Notes are denominated in U.S. dollars, with a $19.03661 minimum principal amount. Quarterly cash coupons equal the reference distribution less an accrued 0.85% annual tracking fee based on daily note value; unpaid fee shortfalls carry forward and may eliminate payments. Coupons are paid in arrears, with the final amount included in cash settlement. The note calculation agent publishes interim accrued coupon amounts daily.

nodes.title: Payment Upon Early Repurchase
nodes.summary: The text explains weekly early repurchases of at least 50,000 Alerian ETNs, their cash-payment calculation and five-day VWAP measurement, fees, coupon and distribution adjustments, and risks of losing principal. It details broker instructions, deadlines, DTC settlement, irrevocability, and expiration of repurchase rights. At maturity, payment is based on adjusted principal, index return, coupons, fees, distributions, and a five-day measurement, with similar loss risks. It identifies the Note and VWAP Calculation Agents and describes how market disruptions defer component VWAP and weighting determinations to a later non-disrupted business day.

nodes.title: Maturity Payments, Repurchases, and Calculation Agents
nodes.summary: Repurchase notices are ineffective if required notices or confirmations miss their deadlines, are subject to the Note Calculation Agent’s validity and delivery determinations, and become irrevocable once confirmed. At maturity, unless repurchased earlier, each ETN pays the Cash Settlement Amount, floored at zero. This amount adjusts principal for index returns between initial and final VWAP levels, any final coupon, accrued tracking fees, and qualifying cash distributions; VWAP levels use specified measurement periods. Investors may lose some or all principal, particularly when index returns do not offset fees. JPMS handles ETN calculations except VWAP-related determinations, which are made by the affiliated JPMorgan Global Index Research Group on non-disrupted days.

nodes.title: Market Disruption Events
nodes.summary: The text defines Averaging Dates, Disrupted Days, Market Disruption Events, and Scheduled Closing Time. If an Index Component is disrupted on an Averaging Date, its VWAP and share weighting are determined on the next non-disrupted Index Business Day and applied to relevant VWAP calculations, subject to a three-business-day cap; if the cap date is unavailable or disrupted, the calculation agent makes a good-faith estimate. Disruptions include exchange closures or trading suspensions, limitations, impairments, or unannounced early closings that materially affect VWAP or hedging, as determined by the agent. Announced regular-hours changes are excluded, while certain volatility-related trading limits count.

nodes.title: Restricted Stock Unit Award Terms
nodes.summary: The page sets out JPMorgan Chase’s January 17, 2023 RSU award terms under its Long-Term Incentive Plan. The Plan governs conflicts, and the award documents supersede prior agreements; acceptance is effective from the Grant Date unless declined by the stated deadline, in which case the award is cancelled. Each non-transferable RSU entitles the holder to one share at vesting, supports future performance and shareholder alignment, and earns dividend equivalents while outstanding. The vesting period runs from grant to final vesting, subject to possible extension and post-vesting share restrictions.

nodes.title: Protection-Based Vesting
nodes.summary: The award generally vests on scheduled dates if the employee remains employed or qualifies for continued vesting under specified job elimination, full career, government office, or disability provisions. The CEO may cancel up to 50% of otherwise distributable RSUs based on sustained unsatisfactory performance, negative annual firm-level pre-tax pre-provision income, cancellations tied to a responsible business line missing its financial threshold, or failure to meet the firmwide financial threshold. These cancellation rules also apply after qualifying termination or potential government-office acceleration. Decisions require Compensation and Management Development Committee ratification; for the CEO’s award, the Committee decides and the Board ratifies.

nodes.title: Bonus Recoupment
nodes.summary: Acceptance of the award makes the recipient subject to JPMorgan Chase’s Bonus Recoupment Policy, including successor policies as amended, for both 2022 cash incentive compensation and this award. The current policy is available on the Corporate Governance Principles webpage under “Other Matters.” These terms do not limit the Firm’s rights under the policy.

nodes.title: Termination of Employment
nodes.summary: Outstanding RSUs are generally cancelled upon employment termination, except for qualifying job elimination, full-career eligibility, government-office service, or disability, subject to Firm approval, required conduct and service conditions, releases, certifications, and other award obligations. Full-career eligibility includes specified age/service, advance notice, performance, and post-termination work restrictions. Death while eligible triggers immediate vesting and distribution to a beneficiary or estate. Obligations include employee and customer non-solicitation restrictions during employment and for specified post-termination periods.

nodes.title: Continued Vesting Requirements and Death
nodes.summary: The text notes that certain age and service requirements cannot be met before the applicable date and that additional notice-period rules may apply. It describes continued vesting circumstances involving Government Office and disability, including eligibility, advance notice, written requests, documentation, and Firm consent. Continued vesting also requires a timely release, applicable pre-termination eligibility confirmation, periodic certification of compliance with employment restrictions, and compliance with the Award Agreement. If an eligible employee dies, RSUs vest immediately and are distributed after tax withholding to the designated beneficiary or, if none qualifies, the estate, subject to local law; distribution is due by the end of the following calendar year, with shares normally registered within 60 days after required documents arrive.

nodes.title: Your Obligations
nodes.summary: The award requires compliance with restrictions on soliciting or hiring Firm employees and diverting certain customers or suppliers during employment and for specified post-termination periods, subject to stated exceptions. It prohibits misuse or disclosure of confidential information, unauthorized media communications, and post-termination access to internal systems, while preserving lawful reporting and truthful responses. It also bars public disparagement, requires cooperation in Firm matters with reasonable expense reimbursement, requires compliance information and permits disclosure of award terms to affected third parties, and sets notice-period duties, including continued service or paid leave, salary and benefits, possible mutual waiver, and a separate 180-day notice requirement for Full Career Eligibility termination.

nodes.title: Remedies
nodes.summary: The award permits cancellation of up to 100% of outstanding RSUs for specified detrimental or risk-related conduct, inaccurate metrics or misrepresentation, Cause, failure to meet termination-related requirements or return forms, or breach of award obligations. Vesting or share distribution may be suspended during review, with no liability for price changes. The Firm may recover the fair market value at vesting of previously distributed shares for specified misconduct or breaches: shares distributed within three years for fraud, willful misconduct, or certain violations, and within one year for listed detrimental conduct. Written or electronic notice preserves recovery rights; recovered amounts exclude irrecoverable tax withholdings, and payment may be in cash or shares, without limiting bonus recoupment. It explains that the list includes parent companies of significant subsidiaries and certain material entities designated for Dodd-Frank resolution planning, while excluding subsidiaries that are not significant in aggregate. The listed entities include banking, payments, finance, securities, asset management, and related companies organized in the United States, Japan, the United Kingdom, Germany, India, and Luxembourg.

title: Exhibit 22.2
summary: Exhibit 22.2 describes JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s guarantee of securities issued by subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Financial Company LLC. The subsidiary issues Global Medium-Term Notes, Series A, under a February 19, 2016 indenture; each note is fully and unconditionally guaranteed by JPMorgan Chase & Co. and offered under a Form S-3 registration statement (Nos. 333-236659 and 333-236659-01), effective April 8, 2020.

title: Exhibit 23
key_items: CONSENT OF INDEPENDENT REGISTERED PUBLIC ACCOUNTING FIRM
summary: PricewaterhouseCoopers consents to incorporating its February 21, 2023 report on JPMorgan Chase’s financial statements and internal-control effectiveness into specified S-3 and S-8 registration statements. CEO James Dimon and CFO Jeremy Barnum each certify that they reviewed the 2022 Form 10-K, that it contains no materially misleading statements and fairly presents financial results, and describe their responsibility for designing and evaluating disclosure and financial-reporting controls, reporting material control changes, and disclosing significant deficiencies, weaknesses, and relevant fraud to auditors and the audit committee. Both certifications are dated February 21, 2023.

summary: Exhibit 32 contains James Dimon’s and Jeremy Barnum’s February 21, 2023, certifications under Sarbanes-Oxley Section 906 regarding JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K.
